Christie’s tepid 21st-century sale caps week of blockbuster auctions in Upcoming York

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1654 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in Newly introduced York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees).
  • Just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%.
  • Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in Newly introduced York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees). That tally fell short of Christie’s pre-sale expectations, which do not account for fees, and projected a total take in the range of $126m to $192m. It was also a lower result compared to the auction house’s last two equivalent sales in New York—namely the $132m ($162.6m with fees) generated across 42 lots last May, and the $99.5m ($123.5m with fees) brought by 45 lots one year ago.

Just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%. Two lots were withdrawn at the last moment, including a Jeff Koons sculpture estimated to bring between $3m and $5m. Twenty-four lots were backed by third-party guarantees and nine were backed fully by house guarantees, representing around 59% of all the works offered. Auction records for three artists were broken over the course of the night.

Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Business began with a bang at Christie’s Rockefeller Center salesroom: the first lot was Roy Lichtenstein’s Small Wall Explosion (1965), executed in porcelain enamel on steel and perforated steel relief to mimic the Ben-Day dot style from his paintings. It sold to a telephone bidder for $625,000 ($800,000 with fees). From an edition of six, it hailed from the collection of Antonio Homem Sonnabend, the adopted son of the late and legendary dealer and collector Ileana Sonnabend (1914-2007) and who ran his mother’s namesake gallery in its waning years. Antonio Homem died earlier this year, at age 86.

Another of the 19 Sonnabend lots from Sonnabend, Ashley Bickerton’s expansive wall relief Commercial Piece #3 (1990), covered with gallery and fashion-house logos and comprised of anodised aluminium, wood, leather, acrylic and rubber, sold for $120,000 ($153,600 with fees). Both the Lichtenstein and the Bickerton were backed by third-party guarantees.

Andy Warhol, Campbell's Soup Can (Turkey Noodle), 1962 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Price points for the Sonnabend trove zoomed higher with Andy Warhol’s iconicand hand painted Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle) (1962), which sold for $7.3m ($9m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. Another Lichtenstein, the painting Large Spool (1963)—a razor-sharp depiction of the titular object that has been featured in multiple gallery and museum exhibitions—squeaked by on the tails of a third-party guarantee at $7m ($8.6m with fees) against an ambitious estimate of $10m to $15m.

Industry observers note that still in the Sonnabend lots, Jeff Koons’s toy-like Hulk (Friends) (2004-12), in polychromed bronze and standing nearly 6ft tall, found a upcoming home for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees). And another Warhol, redolent with Hollywood celebrity, The Kiss (Bela Lugosi) (1963) in silkscreen ink on white paper, sold to another telephone bidder for $3.3m ($4.6m with fees).

Sources indicate that A petite Jasper Johns oil painting on cardboard, Numbers (1957), measuring just 8.5in by 6in and rich in shades of grey, made $2.6m ($3.2m with fees). It was featured in the artist’s first solo exhibition at the Leo Castelli Gallery in 1958. Ileana Sonnabend acquired it from the Castelli Gallery in 1959, the same year of her divorce from Leo Castelli.

The Sonnabend group of 19 lots, including three examples of important 20th-century French decorative art—among them a Jean Prouvé Trapéze table from around 1956 that hit $1.3m ($1.6m with fees)—all in tallied $33.3m ($41.9m with fees), compared to Christie’s pre-sale expectations for the group of $35m to $55m.

Illustrious consignor names continued with works from the collection of the late Museum of Modern Art trustee and patron Agnes Gund sold to benefit the Gund Art Foundation. They included Robert Ryman’s immaculate, small, square all-over white composition Untitled (1961), which brought $2.9m ($3.6m with fees). Vija Celmins’s photorealist oil painting Untitled (Ocean) (1990), which featured in the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s traveling retrospective in 2018-2020, went for $5.7m ($7.1m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. It also was backed by a third-party guarantee.

Vija Celmins, Untitled (Ocean), 1990 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Gund acquired Alexander Calder’s hanging metal mobile The Eye in the Black (1963) from the Perls Galleries in Fresh York in in 1967. On Thursday night it went to an online bidder for $2.8m ($3.5m with fees). Cindy Sherman’s Untitled Film Still #5 (1977), also widely exhibited and written about by major critics, sold for $320,000 ($409,6000 with fees). Gund had acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in November 2000 for a hammer price of $75,000.

According to recent reports, gund’s contemporary taste bordered on the encyclopaedic, as evidenced by an early Robert Rauschenberg work, Untitled (Gold Painting) (1953), in gold leaf on fabric and paper collage on canvas. The diminutive work, at 8in by 8in, fetched a sizeable sum, $1.7m ($2.1m with fees). Gund acquired it at Sotheby’s in Upcoming York in May 1994 for a $55,000 hammer price.

A modestly scaled Lichtenstein work on paper in coloured pencil, graphite and paper collage, Artist’s Studio with Model (Study) (1974), sold to the art adviser Ralph DeLuca for $950,000 ($1.2m with fees).

Jim Nutt, Loom, 1999 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

A standout from the Gund trove, a work she described as “my Mona Lisa”, was another modestly-scaled work, by Jim Nutt, founder of Chicago’s Hairy Who group. Titled Loom (1999) and measuring 15in by 14in, the portrait of a woman with a penetrating gaze set a new auction record for Nutt’s work when it more than doubled its high estimate of $350,000 and ultimately sold for $850,000 ($1m with fees). The ten lots sold to benefit Gund’s charitable foundation tallied $20.3m ($25.7m with fees), squarely within Christie’s pre-sale estimate of $16m to $24m.

Though not part of the Gund Art Foundation offerings, Alice Neel’s double portrait David and Catherine Saalfield (1982) hailed from Agnes Gund’s family and brought $1.6m ($2m with fees). Gund acquired it directly from the artist the year it was painted—not surprising since the sitters were her young adult children.

Alice Neel, David and Catherine Saalfield, 1982 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Recent findings suggest that the appeal of buying a piece of the legacy of storied dealers and collectors did not fare so well for a work that had belonged to the late gallerist Marian Goodman. Bidding on Gerhard Richter’s Abstraktes Bild (1990) stalled at $5.7m, against an estimate of $6m to $8m, and the lot failed to sell. As Richter’s longtime New York dealer, Goodman acquired the lushly surfaced squeegee painting directly from the artist and exhibited the painting in a gallery group show the year it was made. (A second Richter from another consignor fared better, with that somewhat larger Abstraktes Bild from 1991 bringing $7.6m, or $9.4m with fees.).

In a recent development, among the works from more anonymous consignors, Richard Prince’s famous Nurse series made a splash when Everglade Nurse (2003), executed in acrylic and inkjet print on canvas, sold for $3.1m ($3.9m with fees). It last sold at Sotheby’s Latest York in November 2008 for $3.4m with fees, a rather flat return after 18 years.

Large-scale paintings destined to test living room wall space were also in evidence with Christopher Wool’s untitled black-and-white abstraction from 2009, measuring more than 8ft tall. It brought $2m ($2.5m with fees). George Condo’s more than 9ft-wide Double Heads in Blue and Silver (2014), realised $2.4m ($3m with fees). The Condo hailed from the collection of Stefan Edlis and his wife Gael Neeson, who donated 44 works cumulatively valued at more than $400m to the Art Institute of Chicago in 2015.

The top lot of the evening, unsurprisingly, was Jean-Michel Basquiat’s quirky and text-rich composition, Untitled (Leonardo and his Five Grotesque Heads) (1983), which hammered to another anonymous telephone bidder for $28m ($32.8m with fees) against a sky-high estimate of $30m to $50m.

Jean-Michel Basquiat, Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads), 1983 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Evidently inspired by Leonardo da Vinci’s 1493 pen-and-ink drawing on paper A man tricked by Gypsies (also known as Five grotesque heads), from the Royal Collection Trust at Windsor Castle in London, Basquiat’s freestyle interpretation in oil stick and acrylic against a burnt orange background crackles with the artist’s terse way with wordplay and actually features eight heads in all.

Measuring 80in by 80in, the painting has no exhibition history, at least none acknowledged in Christie’s online catalogue entry—though it was included in the Whitney Museum of American Art’s 1992 Basquiat retrospective. The catalogue entry for the Whitney exhibition listed the owner as Zurich’s Bruno Bischofberger, an early and vital champion of the artist. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s London in October 2005, when it was the top lot at £736,000 ($1.3m) including fees against an estimate of £400,000 to £600,000. Sotheby’s at the time identified the buyer as “US Trade” and the current consignor acquired it from that entity in 2006.

Julia Jo, One Fell Swoop, 2026 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

According to recent reports, the evening ended on a sweet note with Julia Jo’s large-scale abstraction One Fell Swoop (2026), donated to benefit the New York-based Coalition for the Homeless. It set a new auction record for Jo’s work, fetching $320,000 ($409,600 with fees). (The night’s other new auction record was for the work of the Spanish artist Antonio Santín.).

In a recent development, apart from that feeling, the outlook was not as rosy. “It’s been a very long week, with a lot of art, and I think people are tired,” DeLuca stated. “The theme of the week is that estimates are a little aspirational.”.

The long week’s last burst of activity will be a pair of day sales at Christie’s on Friday (20 November), after which the US art industry will mark a pause to observe Thanksgiving before migrating south for Art Basel Miami Beach.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti.
  • A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck.
  • According to recent reports, from a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

According to recent reports, from a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

It has been revealed that when you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

Recent findings suggest that immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

Finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

In a recent development, during this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

Sources indicate that need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

Industry observers note that after using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

You can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

It has been revealed that not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Industry observers note that communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

While generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any issues.

Sources indicate that hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Casa Mouda’s initiative includes the launch of an exhibition to mark the opening of two spaces in Lagos – aiMe Gallery at Eko Hotel and aiMe Concept on Eko Atlantic.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Papa Omotayo, Gemma Sfeir and Nifemi Marcus-Bello have helped design two spaces in Lagos for the local creative studio Casa Mouda to host exhibitions that promote design in West Africa.

Casa Mouda’s initiative includes the launch of an exhibition to mark the opening of two spaces in Lagos – aiMe Gallery at Eko Hotel and aiMe Concept on Eko Atlantic.

AiMe Gallery was redesigned by Lagos-based architect Omotayo at the entrance to the hotel’s conference centre, while aiMe Concept was designed with interior designer Sfeir and designer Marcus-Bello in a storefront in the larger Eko Atlantic development.

Both spaces feature exposed concrete walls and columns with touches of warmth, including an earthen bar and screen in aiMe Gallery.

Casa Mouda founder Caline Chagoury Moudaber stated that the spaces, together, were designed to highlight the work done by designers in Lagos.

“As we began to conceive our first chapter of Casa Mouda, we knew we needed to start by recognizing some of the people who had already built so much of its foundation,” stated Chagoury Moudaber.

“There are incredible designers producing on the continent that have done extraordinary work, often taking on alone what usually takes an entire industry elsewhere.”.

The inaugural exhibitions include designers from Lagos, but also those who have chosen to work in the city from abroad.

Among the latter group is American designer Germane Barnes, who showcased his wooden Corona Chair, which features inverted pyramidal legs, and his take on a peacock chair, both produced in Lagos in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

In a recent development, beyond his contribution to the interior layout, which includes permanent seating for the hospitality at aiMe Concept, Marcus-Bello showcased his LM stools and M2 shelves. The works showcase the production possible in Lagos, but also a more modern, minimalist angle for Marcus-Bello, who is known for his massive metal collectible design pieces.

“Nifemi Marcus-Bello has been quietly doing the legwork to set up real pathways for production for years,” said Chagoury Moudaber.

On the more craft-oriented side, the collection showcased works in bronze and wood by craftsman Jean Servais Somian, also produced in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

Servais Somian’s work includes an armoire with gridded screen wooden doors, a console with stacked oval shelves, stools in wood with painted recesses that have a graphic appearance and textural cast bronze stools and side tables. It is an impressive array showcasing the craftsman’s range.

French studio Hall Haus showcased its metal basketball hoops and chairs, a blend of African aesthetics with Parisian urban ephemera, reflecting the cross-cultural background of the studio’s members.

Meanwhile, Moroccan designer Hajar Daide showcased a mix of delicate Nigerian woven wood techniques with lush blue Moroccan fabrics for her Friction Bench.

Atmosphere was top of mind for the designers, and Casa Mouda worked with US musician Malloy James to create custom speakers at the entryway for aiMe Gallery, while aiMe Concept features a listening station.

The spaces have also been set up to further promote craft in the region through display and retail, such as textiles, bags and other smaller items such as jewellery.

“The designers who have forged the way are sharing information on what they have learned; the ones new to this area of production are bringing new techniques and perspectives,” remarked Chagoury Moudaber.

“It has been an incredibly collaborative, generous, and inspiring process – and we are only just beginning.”.

Other recent design showcases include the inaugural Walker Design Triennial in Minnesota and Danish design initiative The Mindcraft Project, curated by Christian + Jade.

Five Ethiopian artefacts restituted in London ceremony

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November).
  • McCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art.
  • Ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November). The process was part of a wider initiative by the American collector Robert McCarthy and the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio that is expected to see many more objects returned to Ethiopia.

McCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art. He broadened his collection in the 1990s to include Ethiopian art, at a time when there was less concern about provenance. In 2023-24 he lent objects to the exhibition Ethiopia at the Crossroads, which was presented in venues in Baltimore, Salem in Massachusetts and Toledo. It was at Toledo that he began discussions with Sophie Ong, assistant director of strategic initiatives, about the future of his collection.

Ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

This eventually led to the new, complex arrangement. Toledo will acquire McCarthy’s 375 Ethiopian objects, one of the largest such private collections. Two thirds will be donated and the remainder bought. Some of this material will be exhibited when the museum’s galleries reopen in autumn 2027 after a major reinstallation of its permanent collection.

It has been revealed that the museum then intends to return much of the collection to Ethiopia, in tranches over the next 20 years. Any items deemed to have left Ethiopia illegally or inappropriately will be restituted. Details have not been released, but it is assumed that this will include looted material seized by British troops at the 1869 battle of Maqdala and which later came onto the international art market.

It has been revealed that objects judged to have been exported properly will remain at the Toledo museum. Stewardship of items with an indeterminate status will be decided jointly by the Toledo museum and Ethiopian officials. It is thought that ultimately half of McCarthy’s 375 items may be returned.

The unusual tripartite arrangement between McCarthy, the Toledo museum and the Ethiopia authorities could prove to be a template for dealing with restitution claims by other African countries. At the handover, Alula Pankhurst, speaking on behalf of the Ethiopian Heritage Authority, described it as “a latest model of partnership”.

In a recent development, this week’s restitution of five objects to the government’s Ethiopian Heritage Authority is slightly different, in that they have been directly returned by McCarthy. The Toledo museum was unwilling to accession them because of records suggesting that they had left Ethiopia after the 1970 Unesco convention.

The items are two 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and three processional crosses. All are believed to have been improperly removed from Ethiopian churches.

Sources indicate that the earliest of the two manuscripts is a Book of Revelation with a Horologium (daily cycle of prayers). It includes seven full-page illuminations, dating from around 1400. The volume was recorded in the late 20th century as being in the Saqqā Madḫānē Ālam Church in Šawā Province.

According to recent reports, the other manuscript is a large mid-15th century Gospels, which includes full-page images of the Four Evangelists. The scholar Diana Spencer noted in a 1974 article that she saw it at the church of Emmaus Giyor near Wafa Yasus.

It has been revealed that ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

The three brass processional crosses being returned date variously from the late-18th to early-20th centuries. Each has incised inscriptions which may make it possible to determine which church they came from.

Industry observers note that the five returned objects are now being sent from London to the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa, where a new display of restituted material is scheduled to open in December. Most of the rest of the display will be material which had been looted at Maqdala.

However, the forthcoming Addis Ababa display may feed into a debate over whether religious items that can be identified with a particular location should be retained in the National Museum or returned to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.

Wondering how to get rid of mosquito bites overnight? Discover simple home remedies for quick relief. From crushed ice to aloe vera, explore easy solutions to soothe itching and inflammation for a peaceful night’s sleep.

If you’re caught without bug bite cream or ointment, don’t worry — plenty of simple home remedies can provide quick relief. From soothing aloe vera to the calming effects of oatmeal, discover easy solutions to alleviate itching and inflammation so you can sleep peacefully.

In a recent development, to whip up your own basil rub, boil a couple cups of water with 1/2 ounce of dried basil leaves. Cool the mixture before applying it to a washcloth and gently massaging it onto the bite for sweet relief.

Its beauty with bites is that it can help ease burning or stinging while disinfecting your scratchy little bump.

Onion juice (while not delicious) has antifungal and antibacterial properties, which could possibly help ward off infection. Plus, it could make your bite sting less. Just dab a bit of raw onion juice onto your bites. The downside? We’re not sure how well it works … and it’s kinda stinky.

Industry observers note that thyme has been used to help with skin concerns for a long time. According to recent reports, peppermint oil may work as an anti-itch agent. Mix it with carrier oil (like olive oil) before applying it to your skin, though!

Another natural anti-itcher and astringent, lemon balm, may be helpful. You can either apply a lemon balm cream or chop up the leaves and apply them right to the bite.

Witch hazel is a natural wonder with many uses for skin concerns such as acne and psoriasis. It can tackle inflammation and burning while helping your bug bite heal.

This herb may work, but the science is a little dicey. On its own, arnica is toxic, so any over-the-counter products you find have been carefully diluted for your safety.

In a recent development, the yummy tea that calms and soothes at bedtime has many other uses, including potentially calming an irritated bug bite. Steep the tea bag for 20 minutes before squeezing it out and applying it to your bite once it’s cooled.

It has been revealed that blend minced garlic with petroleum jelly or fragrance-free lotion. Place the mixture on your bite for 10 minutes before removing it and applying a cool cloth.

Icing the bite for 10 minutes and then placing a mixture of baking soda and water on it for 10 minutes is a strong choice.

Recent findings suggest that though not tested for this purpose, some people turn to Vicks to soothe mosquito bites. Some toothpastes are cooling, so that sensation may offer temporary relief. Some people use toothpaste on insect bites since many toothpastes contain astringents, which can help shrink tissues.

Industry observers note that using repellent to prevent bug bites is a good idea. PSA: DEET and lemon eucalyptus oil are safe ways to repel insects.

It has been revealed that mosquitoes are low-key little monsters that cause the most insect bites worldwide. Most bites aren’t serious, but mosquitoes can potentially carry diseases.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Lv Xiaobin.

Jiang Deng Lu is a house in rural Anhui designed by Chinese studio Shisuo Design Office using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.

Described by Shisuo Design Office as a “surreal rural house”, the compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site.

It sits beside the client’s ancestral home and serves as both a memorial for his late father and a separate dwelling where his elderly mother can host visiting relatives.

“The client wanted to build a house beside the old family home, providing a comfortable place for his mother and relatives to gather and share meals during holidays,” Shisuo Design Office told Dezeen.

Sources indicate that “But beyond this practical need, there was a deeper emotional connection. The old house was left by his father, while the upcoming one represented his own way of creating new memories for the family,” it continued.

“We hoped the house would bring the family together more often, beyond just festive occasions.”.

Jiang Deng Lu’s proportions were determined by the recycled stainless steel offcuts and unused windows salvaged for the project by the client, who is the owner of a stainless steel factory.

“The building’s geometry was strictly reverse-engineered from these salvaged materials,” mentioned Shisuo Design Office.

It has been revealed that “Instead of imposing a predetermined architectural form, we meticulously measured and mapped these specific surplus components. The building’s precise dimensions, roof pitches, and structural envelope were entirely reverse-engineered from this salvaged inventory,” added the studio.

“The resulting structure starkly contrasts the client’s modern, lightweight metal industry with the heavy, rooted legacy of his father’s masonry, translating familial love into a rigorous tectonic language,” the studio mentioned.

Industry observers note that externally, the house is wrapped in a full stainless-steel facade, which the studio mentioned deliberately contrasts with “traditional rural vernacular”. This is punctured by the salvaged windows, positioned to frame views of the river.

It has a rectangular initiative, with a balcony that is suspended over the river on one side.

Inside is a living space, which sits raised above a dining area accessed directly from the foyer. A bathroom and shower room sit off this dining space.

It has been revealed that interior finishes are pared-back, with stone flooring and white walls complementing the cool-toned exterior of the home. Wooden furnishings and greenery seen through the windows add warmth to the space.

According to Shisuo Design Office, the highlight of the interior is a nine-metre-long window that cantilevers 2.2 metres outward, providing shelter for the terrace below.

“The most distinctive feature is a nine-metre-long horizontal window facing east, overlooking a grove of trees planted by the client’s late father,” said the studio.

According to recent reports, “For the client, these trees are more than a landscape; they hold personal memories of his father. We wanted to bring the grove into everyday life, rather than simply frame it as a view.”.

Jiang Deng Lu is shortlisted in the rural house category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Casa Plaj by Extrastudio and Hata-Mazanka Guesthouses by YOD Group.

Another house featured on Dezeen with a distinctive metal facade is Bondi House, a two-storey, two-bedroom dwelling by Nick Kent Design in Sydney.

Photography by Lv Xiaobin.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

L-tyrosine is an amino acid (AKA protein building block) that supports your body, from your muscles to your noggin.

It’s a non-essential amino acid, which means your body can make it on its own, so you don’t have to get it from food.

That being said, consuming foods high in L-tyrosine or taking supplements could have extra cognitive and physical benefits – here’s what to know.

According to recent reports, L-tyrosine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally. Though your bod can prob create enough of the stuff on its own, some research suggests that supplementing with it can boost your mood and help regulate your stress response.

L-tyrosine helps make many vital chemical messengers, such as:.

Supplementing with L-tyrosine is believed by some to boost levels of dopamine, adrenalin, and norepinephrine in particular.

Foods naturally high in tyrosine include:.

In a recent development, L-tyrosine may improve your memory and mental alertness. Since L-tyrosine increases dopamine availability in your body, experts think it may boost your cognitive performance. In addition to reward centers, dopamine is linked to working memory processes and plays a key role in the brain’s aging process.

In a recent development, in a 2019 review of several studies, researchers found that a higher intake of L-tyrosine was linked to improved cognition. It also improved executive functions like brain flexibility, convergent thinking, and reasoning.

However, researchers noted that L-tyrosine is most effective when dopamine and norepinephrine levels are reduced (which basically means when you feel stressed AF).

Some L-tyrosine supplement companies claim that their products are both mood boosters and antidepressants, but the results are mixed.

L-tyrosine increases dopamine, the feel-good hormone that’s linked to reward processing and also addiction. In general, it’s been shown to be a vital regulator of mood, behavior, and brainpower – so it makes sense that getting enough of it could benefit your mood, too.

However, the research on supplementation of tyrosine for depression is super dated, so it’s challenging to draw any definitive conclusions RN. (Plus, depression is also a super complex condition that involves more than just dopamine depletion.).

Recent findings suggest that and though there are some people dubbing L-tyrosine “natural Adderall” for its purported beneficial effect on ADHD, so far, there’s no research to support these claims yet, either. (Though it *is* true that there seems to be a link between ADHD and altered dopamine levels.).

Phenylketonuria is a rare genetic disorder in which the body can’t properly process another essential amino acid, phenylalanine.

Since those with the disorder may also be deficient in L-tyrosine, some experts think that supplementing with it could help relieve some symptoms like seizures or skin rashes.

However, according to a 2021 review of several studies, there is not enough evidence to say for sure.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers taking L-tyrosine supplements generally safe.

That being said, it’s not recommended to mix with the following medications:.

It’s not advisable to take it if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding.

Recent findings suggest that research suggests that L-tyrosine supplementation likely benefits your brainpower under stress. It also may benefit conditions like depression, but more research is needed to know for sure.

Like any supplement, it is a good idea to contact your healthcare provider before adding it to your medicine cabinet, especially if you have preexisting health conditions or take medications.

Nike Tuned Air "a huge stride forward" in air-filled trainer design says innovation lead

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, sportswear brand Nike has unveiled the 3D-printed air bags that will be used for its next generation of air-filled trainers.
  • Industry observers note that “I see it personally as a revolution, not an evolution,” McCartney told Dezeen from the LeBron James Innovation Center in Oregon.
  • Recent findings suggest that tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of Nike.

According to recent reports, sportswear brand Nike has unveiled the 3D-printed air bags that will be used for its next generation of air-filled trainers. In this interview, the brand’s chief innovation, design & product officer Phil McCartney explains why it is a technological and performance advance.

Industry observers note that “I see it personally as a revolution, not an evolution,” McCartney told Dezeen from the LeBron James Innovation Center in Oregon. “It’s a huge stride forward.”.

Recent findings suggest that tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support. Using a combination of proprietary 3D printing and “selective lamination” allows Nike to create midsoles that perform in different ways under different parts of the foot.

Informed by the raised vibrant colours on magazine covers, the airbag is built up from layers of ink.

“We can engineer the structure and tune the structure in the heel differently to the forefoot,” mentioned McCartney.

“We can also tune the height, so you can have a variety of different heights, and we can tune the structure inside.”.

Nike unveiled the technology and concept images for a running shoe today, and is planning for the first Nike Tuned Air trainer to be released next year.

The trainers will be the first in what Nike sees as a third major generation of its air-filled shoes, since Nike CEO Phil Knight worked with inventor Frank Rudy to use a cushioning system filled with gas in the late 1970s.

Following the Nike Air Tailwind in 1978, Nike developed Air Max in the 1980s and Air Zoom in the 1990s.

According to recent reports, “At its core, Air, for 50 years, has been this magical combination of lightweight, cushioned and resilient – it doesn’t break down over time,” remarked McCartney. “That’s why from day one when Phil [Knight] struck the deal with Frank Rudy, we’ve been so committed to it – it just delivers a really unique benefit.”.

According to recent reports, “If Max Air is about maximal cushioning and impact protection, Zoom Air is more about responsiveness and snappiness,” he continued. “Tuned Air, because of this proprietary ink and selective lamination process, allows us to literally tune the sensation within the airbag, which enables us to sort of move free from the constraints of typical geometry and shape.”.

According to McCartney, this change in how the airbags are manufactured opens up possibilities, especially in customisation.

“It is the first step in exploring all the different places that this will go,” said McCartney. “The capability and what we’re able to do with this proprietary ink and the selective lamination allows us to really unlock the real potential of air.”.

“It also creates this canvas for all the design explorations that we’ve always wanted to do, but the limitations of the manufacturing process didn’t allow,” he continued.

“So now the handcuffs are off in terms of it being a canvas – what expressions do we want to explore? What different visuals, geometries, and different ways to articulate the benefit can we explore? We’re looking at all of that. “.

According to recent reports, while the air-filled midsole has been manufactured, the trainer is still in development. However, McCartney expects the shoe to look close to the concept render that was revealed today.

“There’ll be a few modifications,” he remarked. “Knowing where the design is going to go. It’s pretty representative as an illustration, but it isn’t the final design.” He noted that the final air bag design will be close to the prototype.

“What we’re exploring now is how do we take the idea of lightweight cushioning and this idea of tuned [and find] what that looks like in an expression and an experience on the upper.”.

One key design element that will feature in the commercial release next year will be the full-length, visible air bag, which McCartney said is an “vital part of the design and important part of this platform”.

It has been revealed that the midsoles are the latest innovation in Nike’s exploration of using air within footwear and apparel. While it has made millions of shoes containing air, it has also recently unveiled the inflating Air Milano Jacket at 2026 Winter Olympics and its Radical AirFlow t-shirts that counterintuitively use more material to make a wearer cooler.

In all the areas of innovation that McCartney oversees at Nike, air is where he sees the most potential.

It has been revealed that “There’s a number of areas, but if I had to pick one, I think that [air] is the platform that intrigues us most, that drives our creativity the most, that also translates into the biggest athlete benefit. And I mean athlete in the broadest sense of the term – if you’ve got a body, you’re an athlete.”.

Recent findings suggest that “We’re really intrigued and fascinated by the notion of being able to harness what’s all around us to further performance,” mentioned McCartney. “That started in footwear, obviously. This is the next revolution.”.

Photography courtesy of Nike.

It has been revealed that van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees sold at Sotheby's Fresh York on Wednesday night (18 November) for $190.4m, including fees. Auctioneer Oliver Barker began the sale by stating that “the work is being offered for sale pursuant to an agreement between the seller and the heirs of the Hedwig and Samuel Fischer family”. The Fischer family had sold the painting in 1936.

The auction of the Van Gogh opened at $135m, two telephone bidders coming in. A third bidder, in the saleroom, won the contest after less than four minutes, at a hammer price of $165m. He is the Newly introduced York dealer William Acquavella, presumably acting for an unidentified client.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (May 1890).

Before the auction, Sotheby’s had not unveiled a formal estimate range, but instead suggested that the painting should fetch a hammer price of around $180m (before fees). This may have been slightly optimistic, since it was far more than any Van Gogh has ever made. Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890) is a fine landscape, although not among his very best. And the other 11 pictures in last night’s auction of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection generally sold for around, or even below, their lower estimates.

Recent findings suggest that the uncertainty last weekend over a possible Nazi-era claim for the Van Gogh may have discouraged some potential bidders, but the $190m (including fees) was nonetheless an astonishing result. This was for an artist who had failed to sell during his own lifetime. Van Gogh completed nearly a thousand paintings in his career, with only a single recorded sale: The Red Vineyard (November 1888, Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow).

Only three artworks have ever sold for more at auction: Leonardo’s Salvator Mundi (around 1500, $450m, Christie’s, 2017), Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1916, $236m, Sotheby’s, 2025) and Andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn (1964, $195m, Christie’s, 2022).

Recent findings suggest that the previous record price for a Van Gogh was $117m (including fees) for Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888), which Christie’s sold in 2022. The Blossoming Chestnut Trees price was 62% more.

Sotheby’s has been open about Blossoming Chestnut Trees’s Nazi-era (1933-45) provenance. Following our inquiries, we reported in our 2 October blog post: “It was purchased four years later [in 1926] by the Berlin-based publisher Samuel Fischer, and on his death in 1934 it passed to his daughter Brigitte. Although the family was persecuted because of their Jewish heritage, a Sotheby’s spokesperson confirmed to us that, based on recent research, the family was free at all times to dispose of the painting.”.

Literaturport.de via Wikimedia Commons.

According to recent reports, news of a possible Nazi-era claim emerged only five weeks later. Berlin-based Gunnar Schnabel, who describes himself as a “looted art researcher” specialising in the Nazi period, told the New York Times that he first heard about the sale on 7 November, when he was “lying on a sofa in his vacation home”. His letter to Sotheby’s calling for the sale to be delayed was sent on 12 November, just six days before the auction. Obviously this put Sotheby’s in a very awkward situation: should the sale be postponed or go ahead?

Recent findings suggest that in response, Sotheby’s stated: “We are aware of the persecution experienced by the Fischer family. After the Anschluss in 1938, the family fled Austria, and the Gestapo confiscated their Vienna home, library and remaining art collection. But the circumstances around this transaction were different”. The auction house also added that after the war, no claim was ever made for the Van Gogh.

Urgent negotiations were held with the representatives of the Fischer family. The key question at stake was whether their ancestors had been the victim of a forced sale at a lower than market value. By June 1936, when the Van Gogh was sold, the family had just moved to Vienna. They had consigned the painting to the Cassirer gallery in Amsterdam several years earlier, in 1932-33. The price eventually paid in 1936 by the buyer, Paris-based collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer, was $22,000.

In a recent development, comparisons with other Van Gogh sales around the time are telling. In 1935, the year before the Fischer sale, Orchard with Cypresses had sold for $15,000 at the New York auction house Parke Bernet (this was the painting which later fetched a record Van Gogh price in 2022). That makes the $22,000 seem reasonable.

Then there is the Sunflowers (August 1888), which had been sold to London's National Gallery in 1924 for the equivalent of $5,800. Although this sale took place 12 years before Blossoming Chestnut Trees and Jo Bonger, Vincent’s sister-in-law, probably reduced the price for a major museum, it is now regarded as Van Gogh’s greatest masterpiece. This again suggests that the Fischers received a reasonable sum for their picture.

According to recent reports, following yesterday’s Sotheby’s auction, Schnabel told The Art Newspaper that the Fischers had also been supported by the Commission for Looted Art in Europe's co-chair Anne Webber. He added that the family is delighted that Blossoming Chestnut Trees “which hung in the Berlin home of Samuel and Hedwig Fischer for a quarter of a century, has now found a new owner”. They hope this case “may offer some encouragement to other families who have faced persecution during the Nazi era, and that they, too, may find a path toward the recognition of their rightful claims.”.

The terms of the 17 November settlement between the heirs of the Fischer family and the Blaquier-Arrieta family remain confidential. Presumably some sort of financial compensation has been paid. The agreement opens the door for the Fischer heirs to make claims for further paintings which had once been in their family if they come onto the market in the future.

Title page of the Leicester Galleries exhibition Artists who Died Young, with an image of Blossoming Chestnut Trees.

Industry observers note that as a postscript on the 1930s story of Blossoming Chestnut Trees, soon after the Kapferers bought the picture they lent it to an exhibition in London, Artists who Died Young at the Leicester Galleries in 1938. A year after the London exhibition, war broke out. Blossoming Chestnut Trees had been sent to the United States a few months earlier to Fresh York dealers Wildenstein & Co and, after passing through two American private collections, it went to Argentina in 1975, to the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Following the Sotheby’s sale, it remains a mystery where the Van Gogh will ultimately reside.

In a recent development, martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin Bailey’s recent Van Gogh books.

In a recent development, martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

His other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

To contact Martin Bailey, please email vangogh@theartnewspaper.com.

Please note that he does not undertake authentications.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inverted nipples face inward rather than outward. Though usually harmless, it’s best to check with a healthcare professional to get shy nips the all-clear.

Nipples come in all shapes, including inverted ones. If yours are more like innies than outies, you’re not alone! Inverted nipples, also known as retracted or invaginated, are common and usually harmless.

Nipples can range from popping out when stimulated to constantly staying retracted. While usually harmless, knowing the causes and potential treatments is wise, especially if there’s discomfort. Keep reading to learn more!

Inverted nipples mean your chest cherries retract inward instead of protruding outward. They can be a genetic gift or something that happens over time.

Often, they’re just doing their own thing, but understanding the different grades can help you know if action is warranted.

It has been revealed that nipple inversion comes in three grades, according to the level of drama. Let’s break it down so you know what’s going on with those inward-facing nips.

Sources indicate that grade 1 inverted nipples are like the shy party guests who need a little encouragement to join the fun. They can pop out with stimulation, like a chilly breeze or a gentle touch.

These are the least inverted and usually don’t cause any trouble.

Recent findings suggest that grade 2 inverted nipples are a bit more stubborn. They can be coaxed out with some effort, but they’re quick to retreat. They might need a bit more attention, mainly if they cause discomfort or concerns with breastfeeding.

According to recent reports, grade 3 inverted nipples are the ultimate homebodies. They’re fully retracted and rarely, if ever, make an appearance. These are the most inverted and might need surgical intervention if they’re causing any issues.

Sources indicate that so, why do some nipples decide to turn inward instead of standing out proudly? There are a few reasons this might happen:.

Sometimes, you’re born with inverted nipples. Doctors call this congenital inversion.

If your parents or siblings have inverted nipples, there’s a higher chance you might too. It’s like inheriting your mom’s eye color or your dad’s knack for bad jokes — genetics is a significant player.

In a recent development, for some new parents, the process of chestfeeding can lead to changes in breast tissue that cause nipple inversion. Your boobs are trying to adjust to their new role, and sometimes, things get a little flipped around!

While this can be temporary, it may also stick around long term.

In a recent development, there are a few other culprits that can cause nipples to go inward. These include:.

It has been revealed that remember, if your nipples decide to play hide-and-seek and it’s out of the blue, a quick chat with a healthcare professional is always wise to make sure everything’s A-OK. And if there’s pain, nipple discharge, itchy nipples, or bleeding nipples, do so sooner rather than later.

Several options are available for treating nipple inversion:.

Gentle manipulation and massage with your fingers can temporarily draw out the nipple.

While this method can help with mild cases (Grade 1), it often provides short-lasting results and needs to be repeated regularly.

Useful for chestfeeding peeps! Nipple shields are soft, silicone covers that fit over the nipple and help coax the nipples outward, making nursing easier.

They provide gentle and continuous pressure that encourages the nipple to protrude.

These devices create a vacuum around the nipple, gently drawing it out gradually. They can be worn for several hours a day over weeks or months to achieve the desired result.

For more severe cases (Grade 2 and 3), a minor surgical procedure can permanently correct nipple inversion.

It involves making small incisions at the nipple’s base to release the tight tissue pulling inward. It’s usually done under local anesthesia and has a quick recovery time.

If they aren’t causing problems, there’s no medical reason to fix them. It’s a personal choice based on comfort and aesthetics.

Grade 1 and sometimes Grade 2 nipples can pop out with stimulation. Grade 3 nipples typically don’t. They’re super shy!

Recent findings suggest that yes, inverted nipples can be inherited. If family members have them, you might have them, too.

Recent findings suggest that inverted nipples are a common and typically harmless condition. They could run in the family, show up after breastfeeding, or result from an injury or infection.

Often, they need no treatment. But if they cause issues or occur suddenly, it’s wise to check with a healthcare professional.

Photos reveal scale of Trump’s White House ballroom, drawing criticism

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Earlier this month, Trump’s White House ballroom and military bunker laid its final structural steel beam, with politicians and critics weighing in on the scale of the project.
  • Recently taken images of the extension, which show the structure with massive concrete shear walls, steel beams, and columns, along with a partially enclosed roof structure, have drawn attention to the scale of the building.
  • No sign of its planned neoclassical ornamentation has yet been implemented.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this month, Trump’s White House ballroom and military bunker laid its final structural steel beam, with politicians and critics weighing in on the scale of the project.

Recently taken images of the extension, which show the structure with massive concrete shear walls, steel beams, and columns, along with a partially enclosed roof structure, have drawn attention to the scale of the building.

No sign of its planned neoclassical ornamentation has yet been implemented.

Officially called the East Wing Modernization Project, the structure dwarfs the Executive Residence and West Wing.

Trump unveiled the laying of the last steel beam in the superstructure on 4 November, the day after the national midterm elections.

“This is a special structure,” Trump said on a tour on 4 November, according to NBC News. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world, and they’ve been trying to get it for 150 years.”.

It says everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People's House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday. pic.twitter.com/ou23LpAes8.

Since then, there has been a renewed wave of criticism online over the project, ranging from outrage to humour.

Former senator and presidential candidate Hillary Clinton wrote on X (formerly Twitter), commenting on the size of the structure and noting the midterm election’s “repudiation” of Trump.

“It indicates everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People’s House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday,” wrote Clinton.

Congressman Jim Clyburn took a similar stance in a statement on Facebook, noting that the ballroom was “much bigger” than the rest of the White House.

It has been revealed that architecture critic Kate Wagner took a more humorous approach, noting that the ballroom is not neoclassical in construction. Wagner compared it to a Ramada Inn, a chain of hotels in the US, that they will “glue pediments to”.

In a recent development, “[It’s] an outcome designed in a lab to make everyone angry. possibly the most trump building ever built,” wrote Wagner on X.com.

The ballroom has been controversial since Trump demolished the White House’s East Wing in October 2025. The National Capital Planning Commission approved the project in April.

It has faced legal challenges, with US District Judge Leon issuing a stay in response to a lawsuit led by the National Trust for Historic Preservation.

the fact that trump's ballroom is clearly not neoclassical in any way shape or form is possibly the funniest moment in architectural history.

In August, the Supreme Court allowed the project to continue, though the dissenting opinion noted it was “likely unlawful”.

Despite the legal challenges, construction has continued, with Trump’s team leaning on the national security aspects of the underground bunker.

In a recent development, the administration has also floated prepares to add a screening facility at Sherman Park – a small park to the southwest of the White House. Trump also installed a paved helipad on the White House lawn.

#34168. Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year winner named

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2482 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Dezeen ↗ Open Full Page

Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year winner named

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2482 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The wayfinding scheme for London‘s V&A East Storehouse has won Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year following the announcement of all 16 design category winners at a party in London.
  • The 16 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme include designs by Laurids Gallée and John Tree, as well as Foster + Partners and Kettal.
  • Fieldwork Facility’s graphic identity for the V&A East Storehouse experience won the design project of the year award and was also named graphic design of the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The wayfinding scheme for London‘s V&A East Storehouse has won Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year following the announcement of all 16 design category winners at a party in London.

The 16 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme include designs by Laurids Gallée and John Tree, as well as Foster + Partners and Kettal.

Fieldwork Facility’s graphic identity for the V&A East Storehouse experience won the design project of the year award and was also named graphic design of the year.

V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility.

The master jury cited the project as a “sophisticated wayfinding scheme that demonstrates how signage can do far more than direct: it can define identity, shape experience and establish a sense of place”.

The judges praised the design for its “clarity, confidence and restraint, seamlessly guiding visitors through the V&A East Storehouse while adding to the character of the building”.

V&A East Storehouse was up against designs that included a constellation of gloopy-looking polished resin lights, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van and a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

Read more about all the winning design projects below:.

Design project of the year and graphic design of the year: V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility.

Design studio Fieldwork Facility was challenged with navigating visitors to the V&A’s storage vault, including 250,000 historic art, craft and design objects – especially a younger, more diverse crowd who might normally feel excluded from museums.

This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse.

The Hackney design studio looked to an unexpected source of inspiration when creating wayfinding for London’s V&A East Storehouse: Gen-Z apps and services.

“This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse,” stated the master jury.

“As the displays change, the signage, captions and general wayfinding can be updated efficiently, embracing the adaptability and lack of formality of the museum.”.

Furniture design of the year: Dado Series by Allen Kaufmann Objects.

Berlin studio Allen Kaufmann Architekten won furniture design of the year for its Dado series of tables and shelves.

What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial.

The practice adapted a traditional woodworking joint to create a flat-pack range that can be assembled completely without tools nor glue, screws, brackets or other fasteners.

“What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial,” the judges noted. “The shelving is satisfying to assemble and demonstrates everything furniture needs to be, and no more.”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Seating design of the year: Kino by Pablo Castillo Design.

Barcelona-based designer Pablo Castillo won seating design of the year for Kino, a cantilevered 3D-printed chair for Decibel.

Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future.

The designer’s aim was to create a recognisable chair silhouette, while also responding to the specificities of the 3D printing process.

Its entire form is printed from PLA, the most common bioplastic, although the material is reinforced with cellulose plant fibres. This increases its strength, enabling the cantilevered seat.

“The 3D printing of furniture is becoming more refined and this is a strong example of that,” said the master jury.

Industry observers note that “The mono-material construction is sophisticated and has a strong aesthetic profile,” they continued. “Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future.”.

Collectible design of the year: Lima Charlie by Studio Laurids Gallée.

Austrian designer Laurids Gallée won collectible design of the year for Lima Charlie, a series of five colourful, sculptural lamps.

Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship.

The lighting collection comprises five hand-cast resin light works and machined aluminium pieces.

Industry observers note that first, the designer used digital processes to determine each composition. Then, casting solid blocks of the material before colouring, cutting and sculpting them into shape. Each piece was meticulously sanded and polished to arrive at the desired smooth surface.

“Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship,” praised the judges. “Beautiful treasures to enhance any space.”.

Bespoke design of the year: Real Time Schiphol People’s Clock by Maarten Baas.

Dutch designer Maarten Baas won bespoke design of the year for The People’s Clock, a choreographed representation of the passage of time at Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport.

It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers.

Baas recruited 1,000 participants – the majority being airport employees – to form the hands of The People’s Clock and move in sync, forming the hour and minute hands. The second hand comprises a single person running a lap of the circular perimeter each minute.

“This timepiece in Amsterdam’s busy airport momentarily takes users away from the efficient functionality of the space by providing a reference to the time in a more playful and poetic way,” said the master jury.

“It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers.”.

Lighting design of the year: Hoop Table Lamp by John Tree for Vaarnii.

Designer John Tree won lighting design of the year for the Hoop Table Lamp for Finnish brand Vaarni.

There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form.

The monolithic light combines a block of solid pine wood – synonymous with the Finnish brand’s designs – with a hooped shade of thin pine veneer, sourced from a sustainably managed forest.

“We were all drawn to the simple and characterful gestures of this table lamp, which embraces warmth from a common timber,” the judges said.

“There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form.”.

Architectural lighting design of the year: Cologne Cathedral by Licht Kunst Licht.

Lighting design studio Licht Kunst Licht won architectural lighting design of the year for its illumination of Cologne Cathedral’s historic facade.

This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline.

The lighting scheme used more than 700 surface-mounted LED luminaires to transform nighttime views of the world’s tallest cathedral without drilling a single hole in its delicate stonework.

“This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline,” the judges praised.

“The light sources are subtly integrated and have managed to reduce energy consumption while creating maximum impact for this city landmark,” they added.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Surface design of the year: Basic Third by Pretty Plastic.

Dutch manufacturer Pretty Plastic won surface design of the year for its Basic Third tiles.

There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture.

The cladding material was developed by the Pretty Plastic company, started by architecture studios Overtreders W and Bureau SLA.

The tiles, which were made from 30,987 kilograms of post-consumer plastic waste, have been applied as cladding for Plus Ultra III, the first timber laboratory building in the Netherlands.

“Pretty Plastics has chosen to work with the worst kind of plastic – PVC – and found a way to repurpose the material into tiles,” remarked the judges.

Recent findings suggest that “The material is already fire-compliant and UV stable, making it a worthy contender for the cladding of buildings,” they continued. “There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture.”.

Looking ahead, the judges noted “its impact will be proven by how easy it is to scale.”.

Textile design of the year: Bianni Wool Paper by Arudeko.

Mexican design studio won textile design of the year for Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool.

With so much wool waste in the world, this upcoming material adds value to the waste.

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

Bianni can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

“With so much wool waste in the world, this new material adds value to the waste,” the judges commended.

“Furthermore, the processing provides employment to skilled locals, the outcome being an interesting and beautiful paper alternative to be applied to other products,” they said. “There is much potential for further exploration across the world.”.

Workplace design of the year: Area by Foster + Partners and Kettal.

Foster + Partners and Kettal won workplace design of the year for their modular Area table system.

There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition.

Designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power. The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.

“There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition,” said the judges.

“There are sophisticated elements and thoughtful hidden details for integrating technology into an otherwise minimalist design,” they continued.

Product design (consumer design) of the year: Pedal 4 by Minimal.

British start-up Minimal won product design (consumer design) of the year for Pedal 4, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van.

A smart new vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries.

In a recent development, the four-wheeled, pedal-assist cargo vehicle was built to take up less room on the roads and evade traffic even on London’s crowded and complex streets. It is now operating in London with delivery companies Royal Mail and Evri.

“A smart new vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries,” praised the judges.

According to recent reports, “This is a great ‘last mile’ replacement for large polluting vans. The slender design manoeuvres easily in city streets while the electric motor emits no noxious pollutants,” they continued.

“The vehicles’ local assembly also allows it to be easily repaired.”.

Product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year: CurifyLabs PharmaPrinter Aurum by Studio Aslak Siimes.

Industrial design firm Studio Aslak Siimes and Finnish startup CurifyLabs won product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year for pharmaceutical compounding system, PharmaPrinter Aurum.

It’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered.

The system is designed to improve the process of creating patient-specific medicine, born from the realisation that almost 30 per cent of all medication requires personalisation rather than being mass-manufactured, according to studio founder Aslak Siimes.

“This device offers a real innovation in precision healthcare and decentralises the production of pills,” the judges stated. “Precise medical doses are prepared bespoke for each customer, reducing waste and eliminating human error.”.

“Furthermore, it’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered,” they added.

Product design (bathroom) of the year: Dekoda by Kohler Health.

Kohler Health won product design (bathroom) of the year for Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet.

This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions.

Designed to be discreet and intuitive, the tracker clips to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

“This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions,” the judges said. “The design of the device is discreet and visually passive, making it suitable for its function in the bathroom.”.

Installation design of the year: Einder for USB002 Tour by Boris Acket and Fred Again.

Visual artist Boris Acket won installation design of the year for Einder, which featured as the standout show design for DJ Fred again..’s USB002 Tour.

This lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!

The installation features a large suspended sheet of fabric which floats above the audience like a transparent, breathing roof.

Throughout the concert, the sculpture wafts and moves across the audience, creating smaller and larger spaces, static spatial gestures, storms, and water surfaces.

The judges summed up the project as “stunning, emotive, immersive, dynamic, simple”.

It has been revealed that “This lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!”.

Sustainable design of the year: Datecrete by Datecrete Studio.

Architect Sara Abu Farha and engineer Khaled Shalka won sustainable design of the year for Datecrete, a concrete-style material developed by Abu Farha and Shalka formed from crushed dates.

This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete.

In a recent development, the project aims to demonstrate how the abundant regional byproduct can become part of an architectural material language. Patent-pending, Datecrete can be produced as floor and wall tiles, cladding, furniture, lighting elements and smaller design objects.

“This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete,” said the master jury.

“The processing of the pits is decentralised, so it has the potential to scale in communities across the date-growing region.”.

Material innovation of the year: Mimmik Tile by Front.

Dutch sustainability platform Front and biotechnology tech giant Biomason won material innovation of the year for Mimmik, a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete.

Front believes Mimmik is the first bacteria-grown tile to be industrially produced, making a sustainable technology available to a wide market of specifiers looking to reduce the carbon footprint of their commercial projects.

“This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete,” praised the judges.

Industry observers note that “As such, the embodied carbon is greatly reduced,” they noted. “The production is scalable and could shift the dial in the future production of tiles and paving.”.

#34167. Canva's 'AI off switch' finally recognises the backlash from creatives

Canva's 'AI off switch' finally recognises the backlash from creatives

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (756 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that over the past couple of years, most of the press releases coming from software companies have contained announcements of new AI features.
  • In a recent development, canva is one of those companies, and it's introduced a bunch of generative AI tools to its design platform.
  • Sources indicate that canva has added two AI controls for both Free and Pro users.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that over the past couple of years, most of the press releases coming from software companies have contained announcements of new AI features. Image, video and vector generation, removal tools, agentic workflows, AI assistants, and myriad other advances that can help artists do in seconds something that used to take hours.

In a recent development, canva is one of those companies, and it's introduced a bunch of generative AI tools to its design platform. So the email I received yesterday made me do a double take. On the day that Anthropic completed the world's biggest IPO in history, it introduced an 'AI off switch'.

Sources indicate that canva has added two AI controls for both Free and Pro users. The generative AI switch can be used to hide all of its generative AI tools, including Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Expand, Dream Lab and Canva Code. It can be switched on or off at any time.

Industry observers note that there's also an option to “See less AI content” on Canva's library of templates and design elements. This addresses complaints about the glut of AI-generated content making it harder to find quality work, something that's been causing problems on platforms as varied as Etsy and ArtStation.

Canva says AI-generated content remains a "small portion" of its library and that such content is identified in its metadata. Turning on the latest function isn't guaranteed to remove it completely, but it should put human-made templates and design elements first in search results and recommendations.

In a recent development, the addition of a couple of toggles to the UI wouldn't normally be breaking news, so the fact that Canva feels this deserved its own announcement is telling. After heavily promoting AI tools, it's now presenting the ability to turn them off as a groundbreaking advance – and it is. This might be the first time that a major AI-forward creative software developer has recognised that a sizable portion of its user base just isn't into it.

"We believe AI has extraordinary potential to help people bring their ideas to life, and we're excited to keep pushing the boundaries of what's possible," Canva states. "At the same time, like so many of you, we know there's something special about the time, care, and creativity that goes into making something that's truly yours.".

An 'AI off button' is something that some creatives have been calling for. Part of the difficulty in implementing one is that it needs a definition of AI. Programs like Adobe's Photoshop have used machine learning for many years; it just wasn't branded as 'AI'. Many artists welcome tools that speed up their work, but not ones that do the creation part for them, especially if they're powered by models that were trained on unlicensed work.

In a recent development, canva's recognised that. The toggle only turns off generative AI tools, such as ones that generate new imagery, text or code from prompts. Assistive editing tools like Background Remover or Magic Grab, which lets you select and move an object in an image will still be available. Using them won't cause your work to be shamed with metadata identifying it as AI-generated.

A 'no AI button' also requires a willingness from the provider. Since generative AI features are often charged on a per-use basis via credits, software companies generally want to encourage their customers to use them.

Adobe teased some impressive-looking AI-powered tools in the Adobe Max Sneaks presentation last week, but it's also clear that some customers detest generative AI, which has created a market for new tools like the artist-led Niva app, which is promoting itself as AI-free art software.

Will an AI-off button let Canva have its cake and eat it?

You can learn more about Canva on the website.

#34166. Finding, acquiring and showing off: how rich buyers use social media to build art collections
