📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Salva López.

Spanish design practice Isern Serra combined organic architectural forms with a vibrant colour palette for Circl, a fitness studio and matcha cafe located in Barcelona’s historic Eixample district.

Set just below street level, the 180-square-metre space was designed to offer an escape from the busy city centre and contains an entrance cafe, reception area, changing rooms, bathrooms and a pilates studio.

“The project began with the idea of bringing together two worlds: pilates and matcha,” Isern Serra told Dezeen.

“Although different in nature, both share a common philosophy centred on wellbeing, balance and the connection between body and mind,” he continued.

“Architecture plays an essential role in this experience, accompanying visitors on a gradual transition from the energy of the city towards a more intimate and introspective environment.”.

His studio introduced a series of colour-blocked spaces to guide customers through different phases of the interior, with colours that were specifically chosen to correspond to the function and tone of each area.

“This vision of wellbeing takes shape through a carefully choreographed sequence of spaces, where each change in level, colour and atmosphere guides people away from the bustle of the city and towards an increasingly introspective environment,” said Serra.

Serra combined cream banquette seating with dark wooden tables and alabaster sconces to create a calm, meditative environment for the cafe part of the space. A sculptural, mirrored service counter was also incorporated to reflect natural light around the space.

To signal the transition into the pilates studio, the designers introduced a deep-green reception hallway with tiered seating blocks and a spherical light installation.

The bright green circulation area is connected by an open archway and features curved architectural volumes that house the changing rooms, bathrooms and a water fountain.

Another rounded archway then leads to the main studio.

The main pilates studio was designed as a white space to reflect the coloured light from a sculptural LED light installation attached to the vaulted ceiling.

The aim was to create diverse exercise environments and enable the lighting to control the mood and energy of the space.

“The white surfaces act as a neutral canvas for coloured light, allowing different hues to transform the atmosphere,” Serra stated.

“This system also offers flexibility for brand collaborations, as the lighting can be adapted to reflect different identities and experiences,” he added.

In the studio, the designers used mirrored walls to create the illusion of a circular room and added full-length perimeter curtains to soften the space’s texture.

Other interior projects recently featured on Dezeen include Matteo Thun designs for Milan’s Torre Velasca skyscraper and SABO’s design of an apartment on Manhattan’s Lower East Side.

Photography by Salva López.

Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

Industry observers note that the Center for Curatorial Studies at Bard College confirmed Laura Hoptman, executive director of the Drawing Center in Fresh York, as the recipient of the 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence, a $25,000 prize. Hoptman's curriculum vitae reads like a roll call of NYC's major institutions: She started out as an assistant curator at the Bronx Museum in the 1980s and later held curatorial roles at the Museum of Modern Art and the New Museum.

So it is no surprise that, when asked what this recognition signified for her, Hoptman chose to invoke the network and community that her career has grown alongside.

Industry observers note that “The best kind of professional recognition comes from one's peers, and this is one of the many reasons why this award is so meaningful to me,” Hoptman told Hyperallergic in an email. “It also reminds me how damn lucky I have been to have spent the last 30 years around art and artists in one of the greatest cultural hubs in the world. After all this time, my vocation still fills me with joy.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Takuya Yamauchi.

Mexican design firms Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts divided the interior of this concrete building in Tokyo, designed for perfume brand Xinú, with angular black-timber displays.

Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts designed the timber elements as sculptural interventions that also organise the interior of the three-storey shop, which is located in the city’s Aoyama neighbourhood.

The black-laminated wooden planks span the interior walls at jaunty angles, as if puncturing the building, which was originally designed by Japanese studio Satoshi Hirano.

“We approached the project as an intervention within an existing building, rather than simply designing an interior,” said Esrawe Studio founder Héctor Esrawe, who also co-founded Xinú.

“By introducing a continuous architectural structure that traverses its different levels, appearing and disappearing throughout the volume, we intended to generate a fresh perception of the original architecture,” he told Dezeen.

“Both structures coexist, establishing a dialogue between what was already there and what has been introduced, creating an unexpected spatial experience.”.

Long, overlapping shelves with mirrored accents display products on the ground floor, which is dedicated to body perfume.

Xinú’s room scents are located on the first floor, where hand-painted brass panels on the walls and ceilings add a touch of warmth to the concrete and black-timber surfaces.

Aiming to reveal the processes behind the perfume products, the top floor displays botanical specimens, raw materials, found objects and collages in drawers.

Esrawe Studio also designed cabinet drawers to reference the storage and organisation typically found in natural history museums, intending to give visitors a feeling of discovery when interacting with the furniture.

“For Xinú, architecture has never been conceived simply as a backdrop for products, but as an essential part of how they are experienced,” remarked Esrawe.

“Our intention is to create spaces that encourage curiosity, discovery and a more intimate relationship with objects, materials and scent,” he continued.

“In Tokyo, the inserted architectural structures move beyond conventional retail display, becoming sculptural elements that enhance the presence of the objects.”.

Industry observers note that xinú Tokyo is the latest branch Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts have designed for the perfume brand. Other shops include a radial wooden pavilion in Mexico City and a showroom in Oaxaca informed by basalt rock formations.

Photography by Takuya Yamauchi.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nothing in visual culture is neutral, least of all the color wheel itself. Scholar Richard Powell explores this deceptively simple truth in his new book, tackling the theoretical entanglement of race and pigment and how Black painters have used color over time. Trailblazing art historian Lowery Stokes Sims, formerly a curator at the Met Museum and director of the Studio Museum in Harlem, parses his richly layered essays today, linking the critical theory of Josef Albers and Darby English to the practices of artists like Jacob Lawrence and Alma Thomas. The book, Sims writes, shifted the way she’ll look at art moving forward.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, on the other end of the spectrum: News broke that a 1920 painting by Hilma af Klint sold for $12.7 million. Yes, the same Hilma af Klint who described herself less as an artist and more as a channel for a higher power, who followed the guidance of spirits that took physical form through her paintings. But hey, at least the painting’s owner has a latest addition to their investment portfolio?

In reviews, Alina Cohen spends time with the poignant, impactful photographs by Laia Abril, who evokes the systems of patriarchy and sexual violence through the quietly haunting garments and objects in their wake. As the Cornell 7 case continues and convicted abusers sit in office, Abril’s photographs “reject both the invisibility of some crimes and the all-too-visible nature of others.” More, as always, below.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books.

According to recent reports, I was aware of the place of color theory in the practice of art and knew the names of crucial theorists, from Johann Wolfgang von Goethe to Johannes Itten to Josef Albers. But otherwise, I presumed artists’ palettes were the result of personal predilection, technical explorations (i.e., the opening up of brushstrokes and form in the 19th century and the introduction of a wall of color in the 20th century), or cultural orientation. So it was therefore with great interest that I approached reading Richard Powell’s latest publication, Colorstruck!: Painting, Pigment, Affect (2026). | Lowery Stokes Sims.

French architecture studio Ateliers Jean Nouvel has shared photos revealing construction progress on the giant Shenzhen Opera House, due for completion in China in 2028.

Located on the Shekou Peninsula overlooking Shenzhen Bay, the opera house will eventually be defined by an elongated, wavy roofscape, nodding to the site’s connection to the sea.

Pritzker Prize-winning architect Jean Nouvel’s studio has designed it as a new cultural landmark for the city, with a 2,300-seat concert hall, an 1,800-seat theatre and an 800-seat venue among its facilities.

The construction photos help visualise the scale of the 250,000-square-metre opera house, with its various facilities sprawling out across its waterfront site.

They showcase its main concert hall with its horseshoe-shaped proposal, alongside the two smaller performance venues.

Ateliers Jean Nouvel’s design for Shenzhen Opera House was the winning entry of an invited international architecture competition, for which other entrants included MAJOR, Snøhetta, MVRDV and Kengo Kuma.

Alongside the main performance halls, it will contain a multifunctional theatre with 400 seats, cultural spaces, backstage areas, apartments for performers and offices.

To help further connect the building to the surrounding water, the interior is expected to feature iridescent materials such as mother-of-pearl, also known as nacre.

“The sea will be both around you and over you,” explained Nouvel when the project was revealed in 2021.

“This explains more clearly why the main foyer has to be made of a noble, precious and luminous material that spells the meeting of sea and music and light,” Nouvel continued.

“Using the lustrous white reflections of a nacreous material will be a concrete poeticisation of the meeting of the sea and the auditorium and concert halls of the Opera House.”.

French architect Nouvel founded his eponymous studio in 1994. We recently reported on the news that the studio’s La Querola housing development in Andorra, designed with Spanish studio Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos, was damaged in a fire. The project won the housing category of this year’s Dezeen Awards, which took place last night.

Another landmark opera house recently featured on Dezeen is the Shanghai Grand Opera House, designed by Snøhetta with a giant spiral staircase.

Images courtesy of Ateliers Jean Nouvel.

National Gallery of Canada receives major gift of modern and contemporary glass art

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the National Gallery of Canada (NGC) in Ottawa is embarking on a latest chapter in its collecting history with a promised gift of 56 modern and contemporary glass works from Canadian American businessman and philanthropist Charles Bronfman and his late wife, Andrea Bronfman.
  • Industry observers note that “This is the gallery’s first gift of modern and 20th-century glass,” Jean-François Bélisle, director and chief executive of the NGC, tells The Art Newspaper.
  • The gifted Bronfman Collection spans more than a century of glass experimentation, with works by 29 artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the National Gallery of Canada (NGC) in Ottawa is embarking on a latest chapter in its collecting history with a promised gift of 56 modern and contemporary glass works from Canadian American businessman and philanthropist Charles Bronfman and his late wife, Andrea Bronfman. Accompanied by an endowment to establish the institution’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design, the donation will help broaden the museum’s collection and increase its scholarly contributions.

Industry observers note that “This is the gallery’s first gift of modern and 20th-century glass,” Jean-François Bélisle, director and chief executive of the NGC, tells The Art Newspaper. “It significantly expands our understanding of art history, bringing together artistic expression and material and technical innovation.”.

The gifted Bronfman Collection spans more than a century of glass experimentation, with works by 29 artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia. The collection traces the medium’s evolution from the sinuous forms of Art Nouveau and Arts and Crafts to the streamlined aesthetics of Art Deco and Modernism. Early 20th-century examples by Tiffany Studios, Émile Gallé and the renowned studio Daum demonstrate how artists pushed glass beyond traditional decorative applications.

Recent findings suggest that daum Frères, Lamp, around 1905. Collection of Charles and the late Andrea Bronfman Photo: NGC.

According to recent reports, the works also chart the emergence of studio glass as an independent discipline in the post-war period. Additional artists with works in the donation include Dale Chihuly, whose gravity-defying installations are in museums worldwide, as well as the studio glass pioneer Toots Zynsky and the well-known Canadian American artist Laura Donefer.

A selection of pieces from the collection is presently on view in the NGC’s European galleries (until 30 April 2027). Highlights of the installation include Edward Hald’s The Fireworks Bowl (around 1921), alongside architectural works by Tiffany and Frank Lloyd Wright.

“Harvey Littleton’s Red Crossed Form (1990) is another notable work that reflects the development of studio glass as an independent artistic medium,” claims Anabelle Kienle Ponka, the NGC’s senior curator of European, American and Asian Art. “The presentation brings together very different approaches to glass, from the decorative traditions of the early 20th century to the formal and technical experimentation of contemporary artists.”.

Tiffany Studios, Lamp, around 1900. Collection of Charles and the late Andrea Bronfman Photo: NGC.

The international scope of the donation highlights the exchange of technical traditions, particularly the influence of Venetian glassmaking on successive generations of artists, Kienle Ponka claims. Together, the works demonstrate the medium’s versatility across sculpture, architecture and ornamentation.

Equally significant for the NGC is the accompanying endowment, which will fund the museum’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design. The NGC has not shared the sum of the endowment, but notes that the post will support research, exhibitions and future acquisitions, establishing a foundation for sustained institutional engagement with the field.

According to recent reports, “[The donation’s] significance extends well beyond this gift,” Bélisle claims. “The position will allow us to pursue further acquisitions, develop exhibitions and scholarship, and build relationships with artists and institutions.”.

Installation view of works by Lino Tagliapietra and Harvey Littleton from the Bronfman Glass Collection, National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa, until 30 April 2027. Photo: National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa.

Industry observers note that the donation builds on a long history of the Bronfman family’s philanthropy in Canada's cultural sector. “My late wife Andy and I were admirers of the art of glass making and wanted to share this love with other Canadians,” Charles Bronfman remarked in a statement. “With the planned celebrations marking the upcoming 100th birthday of my sister, Phyllis Lambert, founder of the Canadian Centre for Architecture, and the 50th anniversary of the Canada Council for the Arts’ Saidye Bronfman Award, named after my mother, I am truly delighted to be contributing in this meaningful way to the national collections.”.

The NGC has received other transformative gifts in recent years, including a 2025 donation of 61 contemporary works valued at C$22.8m ($16.8m) from collector Bob Rennie and his family. “The Bronfman gift is significant in a different way,” Bélisle indicates. “Its importance lies not only in the quality and range of the works, but also in the accompanying endowment, which will provide the expertise and resources to develop decorative arts and design as a sustained area of collecting and scholarship.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that after 13 agonizing years of waiting for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), gamers worldwide wasted no time tearing up the streets of the game's fictional state of Leonida after it was released yesterday, November 19. The South Florida-inspired game environment is heavily influenced by the culture, environment, and architecture of Miami — from its Art Deco resorts, white-sand beaches, Cuban quarter, and strip clubs, right down to its museums and arts venues.

Industry observers note that as fans embed themselves in GTA 6's immersive landscape, many have recognized real-life locations across South Florida making unexpected cameos. One such case is the Vice Museum of Art, which Rockstar Games confirmed is modeled after the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach.

“It was totally unexpected to see Grand Theft Auto VI reimagine The Bass as the ‘Vice City Museum of Art,’” remarked Silvia Karman Cubiñá, executive director of the Bass Museum of Art, in an email to Hyperallergic.

In a recent development, “It’s a wonderful reminder of how art and architecture can become part of popular culture,” she continued. “Now, I’m just curious: will the Vice City Museum of Art get more visitors than we do?!”.

While not listed as a landmark like the Vice Museum of Art, another building in Downtown Vice City appears to be directly modeled after the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). Situated near the Vice City Arts Center, which is heavily based on Miami's Adrienne Arsht Center for Performing Arts, the PAMM-inspired building sits right on the water's edge just as the museum does in real life.

“We were as delighted as anyone else to find PAMM in what feels like the biggest video game of all time,” said Alexa Ferra, PAMM's senior director of marketing and communications, in an email to Hyperallergic.

Ferra attached a photo someone sent her from the game showing the PAMM dupe and some gummy bear-inspired sculptures installed in the shallow water.

“It's a testament to our stunning Herzog & de Meuron building, and goes to show if you stick around long enough, you'll pop up in the unlikeliest — but inevitable — of places.” Ferra added.

Other references to Miami's arts and culture scene include Leonida's Stockyard neighborhood, which directly channels the street murals and warehouse-lined roads of the Wynwood Arts District. It was reported earlier this summer that Rockstar Games had hired over 50 real street artists to design the in-game murals across Stockyard. Customers shared they've spotted the works of street artist Ahol Sniffs Glue (David Anasagasti), among others.

Miami-raised contemporary photographer Josh Aronson also took notice of GTA 6's inclusion of his installation at the Catalina Hotel & Beach Club in Miami Beach during Miami Art Week 2024, which Rockstar Games incorporated in Vice City's own Catalina Hotel. From Aronson's Florida Boys (2020–) photo series, the photo “Spring” (2024) was made into an enormous sublimated fabric print that hung from the second-story window of the hotel.

The same printed photo, which features a group of cheerful young men photographed from above while floating in water, is shown at Vice City's Catalina Hotel.

Sources indicate that “Florida Boys is my own imagined version of Florida, so I love that it gets to live on in another imagined Florida,” Aronson told Hyperallergic. “The installation at the Catalina was temporary, but in Vice City, someone might stumble upon it years from now. It’s a reminder of the wild ways we encounter art today, and how a work can find fresh life long after it comes down.”.

According to recent reports, GTA6's pre-holiday release comes just before Miami Art Week begins early next month. Those dropping in can find some of Aronson's installations on view beyond Vice City at the Vizcaya Museum and Gardens and the Museum of Contemporary Art, North Miami, and also pay homage to the cultural venues and districts that inspired Leonida.

In a recent development, smiling for selfies should be fun, not painful! If cracked lip corners or angular cheilitis make it hard to smile, eat, or kiss, don’t worry. Check out these tips to heal those cracks promptly. With some care and good habits, you’ll have pain-free, makeout-ready lips in no time. Say goodbye to angular cheilitis and hello to a happier smile!

In a recent development, the first step to healing your cracked lip corners rapidly is to lock in any moisture. Reach for a product dermatologists call an occlusive, which creates a protective barrier that prevents your lip corners from getting drier. Vaseline, Aquafor, or CeraVe ointment are common occlusives that will help reduce cracking.

Sources indicate that dab a little coconut oil, olive oil, or fragrance-free moisturizer on the corners of your lips daily after you shower. Make it a daily habit, but don’t go overboard. A little dab will do. Allow your skin’s natural oils to build back up as the cracking fades. Bonus tip: Add the occlusive lip barrier after moisturizing.

Locking in moisture only works if you have enough moisture, so staying hydrated is key! Keep a refillable water bottle with you as your trusty sidekick. Sip on plain water throughout the day, or jazz it up with a splash of cucumber or another non-acidic flavor. Pro tip: Avoid lemon juice, which can irritate and sting sensitive skin.

Bonus: Staying hydrated will help your raw lip corners heal quicker and improve your skin’s overall health.

Recent findings suggest that have you noticed that moisture is a common theme here? Lend your lips a humid hand by sleeping with a humidifier beside your bed. Adding moisture to the air is especially helpful for your cracked lips during the winter or in hot, dry climates. Think about popping a small humidifier in your workspace or wherever you spend the most time.

It might seem like a quick fix to lick your lips to keep them moist, but that can make things worse. Saliva evaporates promptly, leaving a sticky residue that can attract bacteria and lead to infection. So, keep your tongue away from your lips and remember this: “Licking your lips will cause them to lickety-split.”.

Whether from frigid cold or dry heat, your skin can lose water rapidly, causing cracking, flaking, discoloration, or swelling. So avoid jumping from a sweltering afternoon at the beach into a freezing cold movie theater.

Also, skip the hot showers or cold plunges for a bit. These types of rapid temperature changes will swiftly dry out your lip corners. Bonus tip: Your lips can take a beating from the sun, so find a lip balm with SPF protection.

If your cracked lip corners don’t improve or become especially painful or swollen in a few days, it’s time to visit a board-certified dermatologist. If left untreated, angular cheilitis can last for years, leaving your lips discolored or scarred.

According to recent reports, FYI: Angular cheilitis might not appear as clearly in people with darker skin. Instead of turning red, the affected skin may look pale and have a darker border.

It has been revealed that remember that lickety-split mantra? It’s for real. Saliva can get deposited in the corners of your lips for many reasons, like drooling, smoking, or sleeping with your mouth open due to some sniffles. Bacteria grows in those little saliva pools, triggering an inflammatory response that causes your lip corners to get irritated and crack.

Following these tips will make your lips feel better in about a week. Really bad cases of angular cheilitis can take a few weeks. Avoid smoking and eat a balanced diet to get faster results.

As mentioned above, Vaseline and other occlusives help create a protective barrier over the cracked lip corners, which helps the healing process.

#34138. Threading the Names of Alabama’s Black Belt History

Threading the Names of Alabama’s Black Belt History

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AUBURN, Alabama — In Lowndes County, Alabama, less than an hour from Gee’s Bend, a group of women meet weekly to quilt together in a community center across from Mt.
  • Sew Their Names: Quilting, Creativity, and Activism at the Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art at Auburn University culminates a three-year partnership between the university and the Hopewell Project.
  • It has been revealed that “A lot of the time, when institutions are trying to connect with communities, they’re parachuting artists into a place that already has art and culture there,” Randi Evans, the former Manager of Public Practice and Community Partnerships at the Museum, explains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AUBURN, Alabama — In Lowndes County, Alabama, less than an hour from Gee’s Bend, a group of women meet weekly to quilt together in a community center across from Mt. Willing Baptist Church. In 2021, they began to carefully stitch the names of formerly enslaved congregation members into their work. What started as a project to preserve and commemorate these forgotten figures of history soon grew into a broader collaboration across Alabama.

Sew Their Names: Quilting, Creativity, and Activism at the Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art at Auburn University culminates a three-year partnership between the university and the Hopewell Project. The exhibition showcases a series of handmade quilts by Yvonne Wells, Wini McQueen, and Mercedes Braxton, alongside fellow Lowndes County artists including Bill Traylor, Noah Purifoy, and Charlie Lucas, highlighting the region's rich artistic tradition.

It has been revealed that “A lot of the time, when institutions are trying to connect with communities, they’re parachuting artists into a place that already has art and culture there,” Randi Evans, the former Manager of Public Practice and Community Partnerships at the Museum, explains. “We were really cognizant of our role, to work away from that narrative and work in collaboration with what was already happening at these sites.”.

In a recent development, A transplant herself, Evans hoped to learn about the traditions of Southern artists when she attended the quilt symposium “Every Stitch a Story,” hosted on Auburn’s campus. After Evans heard about the “Sew Their Names” project through a presentation by Judge Susan Walker, she thought it might be a good fit for the Museum in Motion initiative at the Jule. Previously, this initiative supported the 2022 exhibition Spell, Time, Practice, American, Body: The Work of RaMell Ross; Evans herself spearheaded partnerships across Hale County, where Ross’s film Hale County This Morning, This Evening (2018) was made.

Workshops at Auburn University's Rural Studio, November 2024 (both photos Mike Cortez).

“Since Auburn is a land grant institution, we see that part of our mission is taking the museum beyond our walls and reaching out to other parts of the state,” says Christy Barlow, the Museum’s Assistant Director of Education, Engagement, and Learning. Supported by resources from the Jule, “Sew Their Names” traveled around the state, pairing a showcase of quilts by commissioned artists with a series of workshops that allowed community members to participate in the quilt-making process.

In a recent development, the first workshop took place in November 2024, as the exhibition traveled to Hale County, where Auburn’s Rural Studio, an off-campus architecture program focused on rural housing development, is located. The quilts were exhibited at a variety of local venues — what Evans termed a “quilt trail” — including Newbern Library, a project by Rural Studio; Sumac Cottage, an art gallery in Greensboro; and the Safe House Black History Museum, which foregrounded the exhibition’s focus on historical reckoning.

The exhibition then traveled to the Project Threadways Symposium in Florence, Alabama. Founded by designer and textile artist Natalie Chanin, the symposium’s 2025 edition focused on food, clothing, and shelter. The symposium also hosted a quilt-making workshop at the Kennedy-Douglass Center for the Arts in Florence. “Part of the experience of the Mt. Willing quilters is that they also sing as they work,” explains Barlow, who attended many of the in-person workshops. “So the singing is happening, and you have people scattered all throughout this historic house, sewing, learning to sew, learning about this story.”.

According to recent reports, by early 2026, the exhibition made its way back to the Jule for a more permanent place in the main gallery; as Barlow explains, this is an unusual trajectory for a curatorial project. “Most of the time, the curatorial side develops an exhibition, and then education responds to it,” she states. “However, this was a Museum in Motion initiative which eventually led to an exhibition. When you work that way, you have more input from community voices, who are part of the conversation from the very beginning.”.

In a recent development, within the exhibition gallery, alongside featured quilts by Wini McQueen, Yvonne Wells, and Mercedes Braxton, other work by fellow Lowndes County natives was showcased. This included a painting by internationally renowned outsider artist Bill Traylor, a vivid three-dimensional collage by Noah Purifoy, a sculpture by Charlie Lucas, and a poster from the Lowndes County Freedom Organization. By pairing works from their permanent collection alongside quilts by the community, the exhibition emphasizes not only the variety of artistic forms across the region, but also the overt political nature of these practices; the Lowndes County Freedom Organization, for example, fought to empower Black voters during a time of extreme violence and intimidation.

The exhibition soon became a focus of class visits from across Auburn University, drawing students in art history, philosophy, history, and even engineering. “A lot of Alabama-born students may not have a museum in their community,” explains Charlotte Hendrix, the museum’s communications director. “The Jule may be their first encounter walking into a space that can be intimidating; they might feel that they have to know a lot about art. When students participate in the process, you really can’t beat that, in terms of active, engaged learning.”.

So You Want to Run an Artist’s Estate?

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, much has been written about the “Great Wealth Transfer,” a predicted $80+ trillion phenomenon that will enrich younger generations as their parents pass away in the next two decades.
  • For example, when the artist Sam Francis died in 1994, he left over 1,000 artworks, several businesses, extensive real estate holdings, ten cars, and a herd of cattle.
  • It has been revealed that the following text, which touches on topics facing estates, was developed in consultation with experts in fields that serve estates and trustees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, much has been written about the “Great Wealth Transfer,” a predicted $80+ trillion phenomenon that will enrich younger generations as their parents pass away in the next two decades. For those who have inherited — or expect to inherit — the estates of visual artists, the challenges of this “transfer” can be especially complex. Works of art, which can carry both emotional and sentimental value alongside asset value, require special care and consideration. The resulting pressures and responsibilities can divide families and create legal challenges.

For example, when the artist Sam Francis died in 1994, he left over 1,000 artworks, several businesses, extensive real estate holdings, ten cars, and a herd of cattle. His will provided money for a foundation called “The Sam Francis Museum,” but his vague instructions did not specify its activities. Disputes among his heirs — Francis had four children and had been married five times — and the need to extensively document his artwork further complicated matters. Settling all parties' claims and establishing the Sam Francis Foundation took nearly five years.

It has been revealed that the following text, which touches on topics facing estates, was developed in consultation with experts in fields that serve estates and trustees. There are also many organizations doing important work to advance this field, including the Center for the Preservation of Artists' Legacies, the Artists' Legacy Foundation, and Legacy Lab Fresh Mexico.

Recent findings suggest that ideally, estate planning should begin while the artist is alive, with someone available to guide the process and provide key information. Record contact information for key associates, including dealers and others, along with instructions for working with them. The estate will need access to digital assets, including archives, email correspondence, and computer files. Setting up a revocable trust can help the estate avoid probate, allowing assets and property to pass quickly to heirs, and also provides great privacy.

According to recent reports, when it comes to choosing trustees, Joe Oliveira, the sole trustee of the Nathan Oliveira Estate, noted, “Choosing trustees can be difficult, and they may not necessarily be family members. In my own case, I happen to be the most logical candidate. A single trustee like myself can make decisions efficiently and consistently, while still listening to and considering the ideas of other family members.”.

One of the most crucial challenges estate managers face is understanding and cataloging an estate’s full contents. This includes not only works of art but also related ephemera, such as correspondence and personal effects. Unique ephemera, like Joan Brown’s fingerprint-covered telephone on display at her SFMOMA retrospective, can strengthen future exhibition narratives.

In a recent development, stuart A. Chase, a former museum director who now advises estates, suggests starting with an inventory. “In my experience, most heirs have no idea what they have. You can’t do anything without a catalog. You can’t approach anyone. It can be very simple: I use CatalogIt, which is straightforward to use and charges a nominal fee.”.

According to recent reports, when I took Chase’s advice and used CatalogIt to document my art collection, I looked under the bed and found a folder of unframed drawings a friend gave me years ago that I'd completely forgotten about. The app allowed me to print a copy of the completed inventory, which I added to my will.

Sources indicate that an appraisal, an independent assessment of a property's value or condition, is essential to managing an artist’s estate because it involves the IRS. A Fair Market Value appraisal is typically required to file estate taxes and establish fresh cost bases for each work in the event of future sales by an heir. It will contain detailed reports for each object, including artist, title, date, dimensions, medium, provenance, condition, and the specific valuation method used. The IRS requires what it calls “qualified appraisals” for this, as well as for non-cash charitable donations to qualified institutions and other gifts.

It has been revealed that choose appraisers carefully, and select those who are highly recommended. Deborah Gerstler Spanierman, a longtime art advisor and certified appraiser, recommends engaging “qualified and trustworthy allied professionals: appraisers, archivists, estate and foundation attorneys to handle the estate tax filing. Empower them to do their jobs and to work with the artist’s gallery, if they have one, which will all eventually support the artist’s legacy.”.

Industry observers note that artist-Endowed Foundations differ from other philanthropic measures because they create programs that feature the artist’s work. These may include organizing and lending to exhibitions, developing and publishing catalogue raisonnés, or operating education centers.

According to recent reports, christine Vincent, the managing director of the Aspen Institute, an artist-endowed foundation initiative, explains: “Artists' estates and Artist-Endowed Foundations (AEFs) are entirely different things. Artists' estates are typically operated by private individuals and, as such, are not tax-exempt charitable entities. AEFs are tax-exempt charitable organizations with a mission to benefit the general public. An artist's estate may evolve into an AEF, for example under the estate plan of an artist's surviving spouse, but an AEF can never devolve into an artist's estate.”.

Checking an artist’s archive for condition issues is essential. Identify which works need immediate care, which will need future restoration and/or repair, and act as promptly as possible. You might have to make difficult decisions about works that should be discarded or destroyed with the utmost consideration. Seek expert help — from conservators and other art professionals — when works require special treatment or present unique problems.

Where you store work also affects its condition. “Know how to properly store works on canvas and paper in temperature-controlled spaces, and insure them to avoid any future or potential loss,” indicates Jamieson Grillo, the sole trustee of the Estate of John Grillo. “If the estate can afford it, make sure you get your artwork conserved by a professional conservator with past experience and a proven track record in conserving similar art. Also, share any conservation reports with galleries you are working with.”.

In a recent development, galleries with long-term relationships with artists will likely want to continue that partnership after an artist passes away. But estates seeking new representation should start by identifying suitable galleries, looking at those that handle works similar to the estate’s.

Prioritize and prepare before contacting any galleries. Gallery owner Hollis Taggart swears by making it as easy as possible for the gallery by providing as much detail as possible. “The more organized an estate is, the more likely a gallery will be to take on the heavy lifting of representing that estate.” Taggart also advises a clear vision: “Be as supportive as possible by organizing an inventory list of the works so the gallery knows right up front what the estate holdings are, and how big a project is involved.”.

Recent findings suggest that placing works in museum collections helps enhance and maintain an artist’s reputation and legacy. But museums often hesitate to accept donations because of limited exhibition and storage space. Patti Smith, an art collections manager at the Stephenson Ceramics Studio, suggests approaching them thoughtfully and presenting only high-quality works, or collaborating with a gallery to develop a “gifting exhibition.” She states, “I helped develop one for the estate of artist Richard Wilt (1915–1981) that documented a body of his work and displayed it in the gallery. We approached upcoming museums as well as museums that already had his work. Since there was demand for purchasing the work, once the museums made their selections, the work was offered up for sale, and 100% of the proceeds went to the Richard Wilt Foundation at the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art and Design.”.

Estates should have websites that include an artist biography, a timeline, a gallery of works, and contact information. This can help anyone doing research — including appraisers and dealers — and may also help locate lost works.

Sources indicate that A social media presence, especially regular Instagram posts, keeps an artist’s legacy in the public consciousness. Mary Clare McKinley of the Richard Diebenkorn Foundation claims, “When estates and foundations harness the power of social media, it can be a brilliant tool for education, legacy and community building. In my opinion, investing in research is always a good decision. Then, consider the platform a way to share information less formally than publishing a book, and creatively explore ways to use it: Enjoy the flexibility, interactivity, and immediate access to a wider public.” She shares that the Diebenkorn Foundation’s Instagram posts “highlight scholars making exciting discoveries, support museum exhibitions, feature [their] own intriguing archival finds, and suggest new visual connections to Diebenkorn’s work.”.

According to the Center for Art Law, when an artist passes, their estate has two seemingly conflicting tasks: "to protect an artist’s work by exercising exclusive rights over them, and to disseminate their artwork to the public to establish a lasting legacy and placement in the art world.” But this dilemma runs parallel to another matter: Should estates prioritize revenue, or improve public access to art?

Auction results, now widely available through online databases, are key public indicators of an artist’s salability. Selling an especially strong work at auction is a gamble some estates take to establish a benchmark for an artist whose work lacks a previous auction record. Estates of recognized artists may want to partner with an auction house to mount a significant sale.

In a recent development, to do so, an estate needs to meet certain standards. Wendy Battleson, senior vice president at Bonhams, states, “Auction houses, in general, are looking for an estate with an established record of sales at relatively high values (five to six figures minimum), ideally sold publicly. We also look at the amount of inventory available in order to continue to tell the artist’s story over a period of time. The beauty of working with an auction house is that pricing is public, and there is rarely a concern that the art has been sold for less than market rate. With a dealer, the sales are typically private, so you don’t know if you could have achieved a higher price.”.

Breaking: The Venice Biennale's Sham Awards Cannot Artwash Genocide

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1275 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This Sunday, the Venice Biennale will award its new “Visitors’ Lions.” But no matter who receives this poisoned chalice, the results are void.
  • According to recent reports, stripped of the silver and gold they wore in previous iterations of the Biennale, the newly introduced Lions have been thrown to the tourists; “Best Artist” and “Best National Pavilion” will be decided by a popularity contest.
  • “Our exclusion has been thwarted, and the choice now passes to the general public,” crowed Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, whom human rights groups accuse of orchestrating the siege of Kamal Adwan Hospital and the notorious imprisonment and torture of the hospital’s director, Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This Sunday, the Venice Biennale will award its new “Visitors’ Lions.” But no matter who receives this poisoned chalice, the results are void.

According to recent reports, stripped of the silver and gold they wore in previous iterations of the Biennale, the newly introduced Lions have been thrown to the tourists; “Best Artist” and “Best National Pavilion” will be decided by a popularity contest. Why this surprising democratic turn? The expert jury initially appointed to give these honors resigned en masse in April of this year. These resignations were, in part, the result of the Art Not Genocide Alliance’s (ANGA) nearly three years of campaigning to exclude the Israel pavilion from the art world’s most important biennial. After the jury publicly stated their intention to omit Israel and Russia from consideration for the Golden Lions, they were visited by representatives from Italy’s Ministry of Culture. The contents of the meeting are not public, but we can surmise how it went from the jury’s subsequent unanimous resignation. Shortly after, the Venice Biennale Foundation announced the Visitors’ Lions, inviting ticket-holders to cast their vote for awards to be announced at the end of the show’s run.

“Our exclusion has been thwarted, and the choice now passes to the general public,” crowed Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, whom human rights groups accuse of orchestrating the siege of Kamal Adwan Hospital and the notorious imprisonment and torture of the hospital’s director, Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, in 2024. Firmly siding with torture and against principle, the Biennale made it clear that both Israel and Russia were back in the running for the Visitors’ Lions. As Antonia Majaca observed, the jury dared to apply a criterion, and the Biennale responded by dissolving judgment itself.

Many artists have rejected this sham from the start. On the day the 2026 Biennale opened to the public, 54 artists in the international exhibition and 22 national pavilion teams withdrew from consideration in solidarity with the jury. In June, more than a hundred artists threatened legal action unless their names were removed from the ballot. Sunday’s ceremony awards a prize that few want to win.

In a recent development, the massive public pushback against the Biennale also demonstrates how close we have come to actualizing the moral principle that a genocidal, apartheid state has no legitimacy on any international stage. This year, we participated in a series of unprecedented protests. Biennale artists and cultural workers went on strike three times in seven months — nothing on this scale has ever happened before (not even during the anti-capitalist protests of 1968, which put a stop to the Biennale’s prizes for 18 years). This year’s protests were also unprecedented in terms of the level of collaboration between ANGA — which comprises artists, curators, and precariously employed workers — and rank-and-file labor unions.

The Biennale is resolutely global, unfolding in the “anywhere or not at all” of the international art circuit. Against the false globalization of the art market, our internationalism was grounded in local organizing against Israel’s Zionist genocide.

The first of this year’s strikes, on May 8, was built locally in Venice, with Biennalocene, Sale Docks, and other local grassroots unions whose participation provided legal protection for striking art workers. On May 8, 30 of the Biennale’s 100 national pavilions closed partially or fully, and thousands of people marched from Via Garibaldi to the Arsenale, where they were met with police brutality. Many artists in the main exhibition draped or altered their works.

Industry observers note that the second strike, on June 12, was national in scale. It was the result of a year of organizing assemblies and actions in about 20 cities all around Italy, with organizations including Mi Riconosci?, Vogliamo Tutt’Altro, Biennalocene, and grassroots unions through the Cultural Strike platform.

The third strike, on 30 October, responded to a call that emerged from outside the art world from the World Federation of Trade Unions and, in Italy, was taken up by militant dockworkers, including the Autonomous Collective of Port Workers, and the grassroots Unione Sindacale di Base. A network of port unions at 113 in 22 countries, including Italy, France, Greece, Turkey, and Morocco, refused to load weapons bound for Israel. This was the biggest ever coordinated action of its kind, and our role was to help build local participation in Venice.

Today, November 20, as this piece is being published, the International Student Strike brought further strike action to Venice, demonstrating the political convergence between students and the Biennale — students in the city are often employed in the cultural sector under precarious conditions.

According to recent reports, our ability to do this grew out of the work we began in 2024, in adherence to the guidelines of the Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI) and Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS), when our open letter demanding Israel’s exclusion from the Biennale was signed by more than 24,000 cultural workers. That year, the Israel pavilion closed.

Industry observers note that between 2024 and 2026, our campaign connected more substantively with the Italian labor movement. As the June 12 strike articulated, the political atomization of artists is a labor issue, related to the art world’s reliance on precarity, which shifts the risk of political action onto individuals. The Biennale provides no fees or production money to artists, leaving them to fundraise their participation. Those whose work is not sufficiently market-friendly to claw back payment in future sales have to content themselves with being paid in the false currency of prestige.

ANGA refuses the oppressive logic that allows the Biennale to support genocide and profit from precarious labor while claiming to rise above politics. This year, we have made clear that the alliance we have created has the power to disrupt the Biennale’s functioning and change its nature.

Today, the contradictions of the present political order — the indigestible, white-supremacy-coded cocktail of Europe’s simultaneous opposition to Russia and support for Israel; the flailing, ever-dying economy; the oceans of money poured into technologies of death and destruction — explode messily into the supposedly morally hermetic market-world of the Biennale.

The farcical “Visitors’ Lions” are the Biennale’s wager that the walls can always be painted pure white again. But this year’s massive actions have demonstrated that we will not allow Israel’s unspeakable assault on Palestine to be art-washed and ignored. ANGA’s members and supporters are no less steadfast than we were three years ago, when our campaign first began. It remains obvious and undeniable that Israel, the United States-backed abattoir-state, must not be allowed to bring its logic of butchery to be art-washed into neutral “complexity” at the Biennale. And we are now considerably more organized and better connected to the wider struggle against Zionism.

When we look back to ANGA’s beginnings, in early 2024, we remember a time when the shock of total Zionist impunity was still raw enough to feel unreal. We could not imagine that friends or colleagues could disagree with this basic principle. We were soon disabused, as many cultural workers washed their hands of blood in service of their careers.

But our collective efforts have transformed this anti-political status quo. The new compositions of struggle made possible by the mass revolt against Zionism offer a model for how the art world can reach beyond the isolated precarity of cultural labor into new alliances — with students, with dockworkers. The power of boycott as a tool has never been greater. We continue to remake the Venice Biennale, the modern world exhibition, from Walter Benjamin’s “place of pilgrimage to the commodity fetish” into a site of struggle.

#34135. What Does Dark Green Poop Mean? Causes, Diet, and When to See a Doctor

What Does Dark Green Poop Mean? Causes, Diet, and When to See a Doctor

📅 02 Aug 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.
  • Most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down.
  • Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.

Most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down. But if the green becomes a recurring (fecal) matter, it might be something else.

Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.

It has been revealed that spotting green or another unexpected color in the toilet can be startling, but it’s more common than you might think. From dietary influences to your body’s digestion speed, several factors can change poop from earthy tones to other shades. Let’s check some out.

Are you chowing down on lots of green leafy veggies like spinach, kale, or broccoli? These foods are high in chlorophyll, which can dye your doodles green. Chlorophyll doesn’t always break down entirely before reaching your intestines, meaning it passes through your system and colors your stool green.

Sources indicate that have you ever had a St. Paddy’s Day-themed milkshake or a brightly colored cake? Artificial colors in foods and drinks can change poop from brown to green. It’s not magic! It’s just the dye in green food passing through your gut unchanged.

When your digestive system processes food too rapidly, it doesn’t allow for the full breakdown of bile, a yellow-green fluid that aids digestion. This often results in a greenish stool, especially during fast-moving episodes of diarrhea.

Have you recently been taking antibiotics? These meds can reset your gut’s bacterial crew. Since these tiny critters play a big part in the shade of your stool, introducing antibiotics might cause green poop sometimes.

If you’ve had certain medical treatments, it can affect digestion and cause bright green poop. One example is graft-versus-host disease, which may occur with bone marrow transplants. This tricky condition can bring about less-than-welcome guests, like diarrhea and green stool. It’s a clear signal from your body that things are out of sync.

Recent findings suggest that some uninvited microscopic guests like Salmonella bacteria, the water-loving mini parasite Giardia, and norovirus can also be a reason for your poop turning green. These critters can hustle your digestion at an unnaturally quick pace, turning your stool green as they disrupt your gut’s usual rhythm.

Babies can surprise you with a whole crayon box of poop colors, and green is definitely in the mix.

In a recent development, for infants, green stool might stem from the same factors as adults, like dietary changes. This includes adjustments when they start eating solids or changes in a parent’s diet if chestfeeding.

Sources indicate that another harmless cause could be ingesting a small amount of amniotic fluid in the womb. So, if you notice your little one sporting some spring grass-colored diapers, it’s usually no biggie.

Industry observers note that if the green theme park in your toilet isn’t closing down, or if it’s accompanied by other symptoms like severe stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea, it might be time to call in the pros. Persistent changes in stool color may signal underlying health challenges that need medical attention.

Dark green poop can result from eating lots of leafy greens or foods with green coloring. However, it can also indicate that food travels rapidly through the digestive system.

While liver issues can change stool color, they usually turn it pale or dark, not green. If you’re worried about liver health, look for pale or clay-colored stools instead.

If you haven’t been on a kale-eating spree, dark green poop might be from iron supplements or constipation remedies, which can also give poop a greenish tint.

Dark poop could be a sign of your diet or medications. However, if it’s black and tar-like, it might mean bleeding in your upper gastrointestinal tract. In that case, chatting with a healthcare professional is a must.

While green poop can def throw you through a loop, it’s usually not a sign of anything serious. It’s often your body’s way of dealing with what you eat or how fast you digest. So, unless it’s paired with other worrying symptoms, there’s probably no need to panic.

#34134. In a Midtown Office, Artists Sift Through the Junkspace of Capitalism

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1628 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hyperallergic ↗ Open Full Page

In a Midtown Office, Artists Sift Through the Junkspace of Capitalism

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1628 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A few hours before 260 Madison opened on September 24, I trekked to its namesake address in Midtown to meet the curators.
  • Recent findings suggest that the three artists-turned-curators, Shaina Tabak, Dayana Matasheva, and Edson Niebla Rodríguez (the latter two of whom make up the duo DemonLovers Inc.), organized 260 Madison as an intergenerational, “inter-everything” show with work by over 50 artists, including self-taught and non-traditionally educated practitioners.
  • Upon entering the first room on the left, I was immediately met with artist Jon Kessler’s towering nine-foot-tall sculpture, in which four plastic male dolls in Adidas tracksuits dangled from a weighted contraption somewhere between a carnival ride and a torture device.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A few hours before 260 Madison opened on September 24, I trekked to its namesake address in Midtown to meet the curators. A security guard directed me to the 14th floor of the 1950s office building, where drop ceilings, an exposed HVAC system, and two people I assumed were the exhibition organizers dressed in corporate drag greeted me. They quickly clarified they were not; they were from AmTrustRE, the real estate manufacturer that offered the derelict 23,000-square-foot office space to the artists for free while preparing it — and three other unoccupied floors — for their next corporate tenants.

Recent findings suggest that the three artists-turned-curators, Shaina Tabak, Dayana Matasheva, and Edson Niebla Rodríguez (the latter two of whom make up the duo DemonLovers Inc.), organized 260 Madison as an intergenerational, “inter-everything” show with work by over 50 artists, including self-taught and non-traditionally educated practitioners. On view through this Sunday, November 22, the show arrives just as the Whitney Museum of American Art opens artport: A History of Internet Art, signaling a new wave of institutional recognition for internet-grown art. With 260 Madison artists Maya Man, Rachel Rossin, and Eva and Franco Mattes among those included in the Whitney’s 25th-anniversary exhibition for its net art commissioning platform, the Midtown show feels especially urgent, if only because it takes place at the precipice of a paradigmatic shift within the art world.

Upon entering the first room on the left, I was immediately met with artist Jon Kessler’s towering nine-foot-tall sculpture, in which four plastic male dolls in Adidas tracksuits dangled from a weighted contraption somewhere between a carnival ride and a torture device. Titled “It Takes a Global Village Idiot” (2018) after philosopher Marshall McLuhan’s early ’60s theory that information-age technology “recreates the world in the image of a global village,” the sculpture forces viewers to confront the fact that the quick fixes of amusement proffered by technology rely on the same methods of data extraction that undergird systemic violence. It’s an unsettling introduction to a show where, even in its more humorous, delusionally conspiratorial, or enchanting moments, discomfort is always in the periphery.

Recent findings suggest that “We don’t want to make a show or art that tries to be some form of escapism,” Rogríguez told Hyperallergic during an interview the week after the opening. “It’s like the [Werner Herzog] quote, ‘The poet must not avert his eyes.’ If some art in the show seems depressing, it’s because we live in what seems a depressing time.”.

It has been revealed that rodríguez and Matasheva, who are also a couple, began making work together seven years ago while studying film in Montreal. Their video-art duo is named after Olivier Assayas’s 2002 film Demonlover, where multiple global corporations compete for a new immersive Japanese hentai manufacturer through extreme methods of espionage, exploitation, and blackmail.

“DemonLovers is about the libidinal economy and how algorithms are weaponizing our very basic instincts and desires,” Matasheva told Hyperallergic, echoing Rodríguez’s interest in what he calls “financial Freud,” or the psychoanalytic dimension of digital capital flows.

Sources indicate that both DemonLovers’s own two works in the show and those they curated certainly don’t shy away from the degradation associated with extractive economies, be it of the self, physical infrastructure, or the proverbial global village. Nearby Kessler’s work, Theresa Tomi Faison’s “The Long Tail” (2026) climbs up one of the floor’s load-bearing columns. Across the curved sculpture’s six screens, images of memes, forum screenshots, and phrases ruminating on contemporary capital flow all accumulate and dissolve downstream. The river of digital spam ends at the viewer’s feet, inculcating the audience, but also the space itself, which the curators characterize as shaped by "junkspace” — architect Rem Koolhaas's term for fallout that “remains after modernization has run its course.”.

Among works that are either readymades or play with the form’s history — including Anthony Discenza’s windowsill pile of unopened credit card and loan offer letters in “Offers” (2026) and Eva and Franco Mattes’s distended taxidermied cat, “Longcat” (2026) — the corporate detritus can be difficult to parse from the artistic interventions. At one point, I mistook a few square feet of wallpaper with the Champion logo for a upcoming work. The curators clarified during a later conversation that it was actually kept from the office’s previous tenants, HanesBrands, which owns Champion.

Industry observers note that having also inherited the space’s trove of gutted bathrooms, broken drywall, and stripped concrete floors (in short, its junkspace), the curators stated they view 260 Madison through “layers of site responsiveness” more than anything. With some works, that connection emerged during the eleventh hour of installation. With others, the site occasioned the work itself. Ivana Dama used exposed air vents for “The Air Was Already Here” (2026), a sound work that channels air through reeds, transforming the invisible, inaudible rhythms of the space into what the artist describes as a “sculptural presence.” Pictures Generation artist Matt Mullican took a 47-foot span of unused wall space as an opportunity to reflect on his five-decade practice of constructing, deconstructing, and classifying systems of representation and perception with largely nonverbal symbols.

“He spent three days here drawing his entire practice on the wall, right from the beginning to the end,” Matasheva stated regarding Mullican’s monumental graphite piece, “Representing The Work” (2026). “He said he will give a lecture about it and that it's a very vital work for him. It's kind of a conclusion of his practice.”.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, the show’s video works are lodged into broken columns, ceiling alcoves, liminal backrooms, bathroom plumbing, abstract paintings, and even a hanging pink punching bag, a veritable reunion of the last decade of post-internet art movements. Alumni from Joshua Citarella’s publishing platform Do Not Research, the New Museum-affiliated Rhizome, and the traveling video and film screening series Open Secret, including Faison, Dana Dawud, Yehwan Song, and Ruba Al-Sweel, have contributed works. Many of them feature themes of surveillance, internet-induced conspiracy, and social media performance, as well as the technological, often AI-abetted methods of production that have come to define such enclaves.

It has been revealed that yet, for all the immateriality and speculative knowledge that flows through these works, 260 Madison equally plumbs an idea of technology with a long, craft-driven history. Tabak, a sculptor with a background in furniture design, is the driving force behind this facet of the show — and the currents of divination, enchantment, and even sublimity that come with it.

It has been revealed that “My practice is very handmade and material-focused, so I always know that that’s what I would contribute to the curatorial vision,” Tabak told Hyperallergic. “And just being in Midtown, you shouldn’t separate a show from what’s happening around it.

Tabak was particularly interested in curating works that “blur the line between the hand and technology,” inviting artists who “haven’t had a lot of chances to show in art contexts, whether it’s because they are in the design world or have nine-to-fives,” to participate in the exhibition. She explains that many of them complicate the very notion of technology and its use, citing Brian Oakes’s “Vessel 9” (2025), which gathers 3D-modeled circuit boards into a suspended “techno-Gothic” chandelier, and Ryan Decker’s “The Wavemaker Falters” (2026), which uses a motorized, rudder-like instrument to swoosh water through a raised vessel resembling a spaceship.

“We view technology not as something that has arrived in the 20th century, but something that has made humanity possible,” Matasheva remarked, expanding on Tabak’s comment. “Language is a technology, a chisel is a technology, everything is a technology.”.

While many of the show’s craft-driven works conjure the anthropologist Alfred Gell’s idea that art is a technology that enchants, and in turn, becomes enchanted, others wield technology in the service of care. Kylie Mitchell repurposes a light-seeking solar robot and discarded electronic parts to move a found bird’s nest and egg toward a life-sustaining heat lamp. A few dozen feet away, Gregory Kalliche’s installation “Black-tailed gull nest; Ring-necked Pheasant Nest; Mallard Nest” (2016) suspends an LED light over three metal folding chairs printed with images of bird egg nests. Ben Gould’s “Ark II” (2026), on the other hand, augments a hospital gurney with eight aluminum armatures that hold fresh red roses inside coil-shaped glass vials. Doubling as a literal manifestation of Shakespeare’s “this mortal coil” phrase in Hamlet, the sculpture’s sterile infrastructure butts against the transitory visual comfort proffered by its flowers, mirroring a healthcare ecosystem wherein privatization, optimization, and tech automation have whittled medicine’s promises of care, healing, and empathy into mere aesthetic veneers.

It’s no coincidence that many of the works in 260 Madison position technology as both a pathogen and cure for today’s cultural ailments. In fact, when the real estate developers initially contacted Columbia University’s School of the Arts, it was to invite artists to “activate” a 36,000-square-foot gutted Duane Reade on the building’s ground floor. The developers eventually retracted their offer and moved the exhibition to the 14th floor, citing ongoing construction. Meanwhile, the original initiative for 260 Madison to occupy the husk of the Duane Reade will be realized in a different form next month. Now serving as the building’s new temporary lobby, the former pharmacy will play host to a different group exhibition curated independently by Tabak. Opening December 3, HOW I FEEL will feature artists working across sculpture, social architecture, photography, painting, performance, and programming, including Jessica Vaughn, Quay Quinn Wolf, André Magaña, and 260 Madison’s Grayson Cox and Luke Murphy. How the forthcoming Duane Reade show contends with this moment of tech-induced economic entropy, so intense that even an entity as extractive as a real-estate tech giant cannot commit to its own speculations, remains to be seen.

GTA 6's environmental storytelling is hidden in the details you might never notice

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best environmental storytelling in video games doesn’t always hit you in the face and demand you stop to look, and GTA 6 has perfected that.
  • Rockstar’s developers say that kind of discovery is central to Grand Theft Auto 6, a world designed to reward players who take their time.
  • In a recent development, “The life is in the detail of Grand Theft Auto VI,” claims Adam Cochrane, Vice President of Art: Environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best environmental storytelling in video games doesn’t always hit you in the face and demand you stop to look, and GTA 6 has perfected that. Sometimes it’s a carefully dressed room, an overgrown garden, or a detail you spot out of the corner of your eye while heading somewhere else.

Rockstar’s developers say that kind of discovery is central to Grand Theft Auto 6, a world designed to reward players who take their time. After three weeks of playing GTA 6, I'd say the world-building is some of the best, most detailed, and most nuanced I've experienced. It can be as small as mud on a character's trainers, a branded coffee mug, or a car decal.

In a recent development, “The life is in the detail of Grand Theft Auto VI,” claims Adam Cochrane, Vice President of Art: Environment. “The subtle sway of trees or bunting swaying in the wind. A puddle of bin juice around the bottom of a dumpster, or an overgrown garden in a property that is unoccupied.”.

It’s the sort of detail that makes a place feel inhabited rather than assembled for a game. Cochrane points to the personalisation of homes and businesses, and the little vignettes the teams have added for players to discover. Some offer in-game rewards; others are there simply to be found.

“Then you zoom out, and you look at the sheer scale of the world, and you realise that the detail you’ve been discovering on such a small scale is quite literally everywhere across the vast landscape of this world,” he notes. “Then you realise that it’s all been curated, considered, and created by a human hand, and you can’t quite believe it.”.

That thinking extends beyond what you can see. Steven Messinger, Senior Design Director: Open World, explains that Rockstar has built deep backstories for things players may only glimpse. The game’s gang compounds, for example, have a fully mapped drug network, from supply routes to street-level buyers.

“Players will only pick up on bits and pieces of this,” Messinger notes, “but having that structure in the background as something we consistently refer to helps everything feel more real, like this massive machine is always running even when players aren’t there.”.

In a recent development, it’s a huge amount of work for details many players may miss. That’s rather the point.

Industry observers note that ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian released Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

Breaking: SSdH "renegotiates light" in Melbourne warehouse transformation

💡 Key Takeaways

  • For the project, SSdH wanted to focus on adaptation over replacement and aimed to work as much as possible with the existing warehouse structure.
  • The studio designed a raised courtyard, a steel-mesh external stair tower and a double-height atrium to draw more natural light into the 770-square-metre space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Pier Carthew.

A double-height glass atrium draws light into the open-proposal interior of Tucker, a former warehouse that Australian architecture practice SSdH has turned into a residence and exhibition space in Melbourne.

For the project, SSdH wanted to focus on adaptation over replacement and aimed to work as much as possible with the existing warehouse structure.

The studio designed a raised courtyard, a steel-mesh external stair tower and a double-height atrium to draw more natural light into the 770-square-metre space.

To help retain the character of the former warehouse, SSdH fitted the main entrance into its loading bay and preserved a ghost sign overhead.

The Galvabond-clad entry was designed to act as a “deliberately compressed” holding zone, SSdH said, suspending visitors within a relatively unlit area before opening onto the light-drenched central space.

“Light was a significant part of the original brief, with the existing boundary walls, limited openings and previous additions leaving much of the warehouse interior quite dark”, SSdH told Dezeen.

“We liked the idea of being held for a moment, making the shift in scale and light feel more surprising”.

Next to the main entrance, SSdH placed a double-storey external stairway that leads to a roof terrace. This was clad in steel mesh to allow for natural light and views from the first-floor interiors.

The ground floor interior is dominated by a double-height glass and steel atrium that was angled against the original floor initiative of the warehouse to let light into the open-plan living area.

“Our approach begins with looking at what’s already there rather than trying to make something entirely upcoming”, SSdH mentioned.

“We were interested in how the building could continue to evolve through smaller adjustments rather than extensive demolition”.

The studio designed the interior of the home to be “continuously adaptable”, with the ground floor able to be used as an exhibition space.

Much of the floor plan is given over to open space, with a curation of select furnishings anchoring it.

In the living area, built-in sofas line the perimeter of the atrium wall next to the courtyard, and are accompanied by an industrial-informed timber and shearling bench by design studio BMDO.

In the kitchen, SSdH added a monolithic travertine island that is complemented by spotted-gum-timber and stainless-steel cabinetry that was fitted against a preserved painted-brick wall.

“Throughout, the material palette is honest, refined and robust, allowing the characters of the original warehouse to remain present”, remarked SSdH.

A wooden staircase set within a double-height void leads to the first floor, which features wraparound circulation and is home to the private bedrooms and bathrooms.

Industry observers note that spotted-gum and big-river timber cladding was used across cabinetry, extended doorways and flooring, with exposed roof trusses visible throughout. Both bedrooms receive ample light from south and north-facing windows, with the primary bedroom overlooking the atrium and courtyard below.

The main bathroom is fitted with wraparound marble and features a glass brick exterior wall that SSdH added as part of its aim to “renegotiate light” within the existing framework of the warehouse.

“We were drawn to the thickness and form of the glass, which catches, holds and releases light in a way that conventional textured glazing doesn’t quite achieve,” the studio said.

Overall, SSdH hoped to preserve the charm of the original warehouse while creating an adaptable, contemporary space.

Many decisions were “made on site as the building revealed itself”, the studio noted.

“We wanted the spaces to remain open to different ways and possibilities of living, allowing the building to adapt without needing to be completely reworked in the future”, it concluded.

Other Melbourne homes recently featured on Dezeen include a studio with a “lantern-like” glass-block facade, a century-old corner shop transformed into a family home and a home comprised of a cluster of red-brick volumes.

Photography by Pier Carthew.

💡 Key Takeaways
