  • Industry observers note that the US Department of State’s Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation (AFCP) financed the work at the Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas church, located in the Andes mountains at almost 4,000m above sea level.
  • Recent findings suggest that “The Curahuara church has great value because of its paintings, so it’s essential that the roof is in good condition to prevent leaks that could compromise the murals,” Josefina Matas, the architect in charge of the project, tells The Art Newspaper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of Bolivia’s oldest churches, known as the “Sistine Chapel of the Andes” due to its impressive murals, is nearing completion of a conservation project focused on its roofs, stone buttresses and adobe walls—a process that began in May.

Industry observers note that the US Department of State’s Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation (AFCP) financed the work at the Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas church, located in the Andes mountains at almost 4,000m above sea level. Approximately 170km west of the city of Oruro, the church was declared a National Monument in 1960.

Recent findings suggest that “The Curahuara church has great value because of its paintings, so it’s essential that the roof is in good condition to prevent leaks that could compromise the murals,” Josefina Matas, the architect in charge of the project, tells The Art Newspaper. This work follows restoration that took place more than a decade ago, funded by the German embassy in La Paz.

The restoration team has had to learn the church’s unique roof-building technique from locals, placing straw on top of hollow cane mats using a method that makes it more resilient. Hollow cane is hard to find in the highlands, so they needed to bring it in from Bolivia’s southernmost region of Tarija.

Working on the church’s new roofs Courtesy US Embassy in Bolivia.

Sources indicate that during the previous restoration, corrugated metal sheets had been added to extend the lifespan of the roofs, which cover 800 sq. m. This time, workers replaced the damaged sections. The project was delayed because of proteststhat blocked roads across the country in May and June, preventing the arrival of materials and postponing its completion by one month—from the end of October to the end of November.

Built by Augustinians between the late 16th and early 17th centuries, the church houses paintings of the Nativity, the Last Supper, the Crucifixion and the Last Judgment in a display of religious syncretism. “It’s a complete catechesis,” Matas indicates of the murals, which were made using natural dyes and finished in 1777.

In a recent development, there are also representations of the apostle Santiago (James), the church’s patron saint. Local Indigenous people identified him with Illapa, the Inca god of thunder. The style of the paintings ranges from Mannerism to 18th-century Baroque, with depictions of birds and flowers—an example of mestizo art.

“It’s very striking when you enter the church, because there isn’t any empty space,” Matas indicates. “Everything is painted.” The paintings even cover the baptistery and sacristy. “Most of the churches in the region have murals. Here, they have been well preserved,” she adds.

Restoration underway at Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas Courtesy US Embassy in Bolivia.

The building has a single entrance through a side wall, similar to other churches in the area, and is surrounded by an atrium with two gates. “Indigenous people weren’t used to entering the building for religious activities, so the atrium was spacious enough to accommodate those who wanted to be evangelised,” Matas states.

Industry observers note that the bishop of Oruro, Krzysztof Białasik, was the one who submitted the restoration project to compete for US funding. Since 2001, the AFCP has financed more than 30 projects in Bolivia, including the restoration of colonial paintings, the protection of Baroque musical manuscripts and the creation of a digital catalogue—including archaeological artefacts, pre-Columbian textiles and colonial art—available to customs services to curb the illicit trafficking of these goods.

To celebrate the completion of the conservation of the church, a mass will be held in Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas with the bishop and the apostolic nuncio on 15 December.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Patricia Belli, Troy Montes Michie, Willy Chavarria, and Camila Falquéz are among the 20 artists and designers who will be featured in Malvestir, MoMA PS1's upcoming exhibition on the visual lexicon of Latin American fashion, opening in April 2027.

Recent findings suggest that A portmanteau of the Spanish words mal (poorly) and vestir (to dress), Malvestir features creatives across the Americas who probe the historical and contemporary resonances of Latin American dress. Western appropriations of Indigenous crafts, exorbitant textile waste, and the fetishization of Latin American styles are just some of the key concerns that will be interrogated in the exhibition.

Curated by MoMA PS1 director Connie Butler and associate curator Elena Ketelsen González, Malvestir will include a range of artists, from Newly introduced York City designers to textile artists reinvigorating intergenerational weaving traditions.

In a recent development, several designers are striving to reclaim styles and symbols co-opted by mainstream Western markets. Known for his oversized proportions and street-style designs emblematic of the Mexican-American fashion tradition, New York designer Willy Chavarria is showing Safe From Home (2024), a film that expanded upon themes of love and the right to safety explored in his Autumn/Winter 2024 collection. Malvestir will also include the work of designer Carla Fernández, who nurtures collaborations with local artisans in Mexico to preserve Indigenous motifs against corporate reproduction and profiteering.

Recent findings suggest that works from multimedia artists who use photography, drawing, painting, sculpture, and textiles to preserve intergenerational customs will also be on view. Latest Mexico-based artist Josh Tafoya revitalizes his family’s weaving tradition through the centuries-long practice of Rio Grande loom weaving. David Ramirez Cotón pays homage to Guatemalan fashion with a series of hyperrealistic acrylic-on-canvas paintings cut to resemble articles of clothing hanging from a rack in a second-hand shop.

The exhibition comes at a time when Latin American communities are facing regressive crackdowns from multiple parties — the federal government, exploitative corporations, and immigration enforcement. Yet it has also prompted many to recognize the importance of Latinx artists through displaying the full range and power of their respective cultures, as mainstream appropriation and demands for assimilation reach fresh, threatening extremes.

In an opinion for Hyperallergic this month, Arlene Dávila, a professor of anthropology and American Studies at New York University, positioned the current political climate as a rallying cry for Latinx visionaries.

Within her essay, she referenced Chavarria and Raul Lopez (founder of LUAR), two of the artists whose work will appear in Malvestir, underscoring how they "frequently use street-cast Black and Brown models to communicate a richer, more inclusive vision beyond traditional, Eurocentric runways.".

"Across these fields, artists are choosing to create work that is deeply rooted in their communities, drawing directly from vernacular traditions, oral histories, and family memories that were once pushed to the margins," Dávila wrote. "While they recognize there are no guarantees of commercial or institutional rewards, their work stems from a shared conviction: We have rich cultures to offer, and we will tell our stories by any means necessary.".

Is GTA VI the Art Miami Deserves?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4321 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SIGNIFICANTLY less cars on the road.” The text from Miami-based artist, educator, and organizer misael soto sent yesterday, November 19, a few hours after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, encapsulated many of my complicated feelings about the long-awaited game.
  • Industry observers note that the premise of GTA VI is simple on the surface.
  • According to recent reports, to help make sense of these tensions, I got on a phone call with soto and Leo Castañeda, two Miami-based artists whose work I admire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Driving at rush hour. SIGNIFICANTLY less cars on the road.” The text from Miami-based artist, educator, and organizer misael soto sent yesterday, November 19, a few hours after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, encapsulated many of my complicated feelings about the long-awaited game. We’d come full circle: The traffic hell that Miami, the city I once called home, has now become notorious for — in no small part due to overdevelopment, climate change, and strained infrastructure — was being alleviated by a video game that kept people at home, inside a simulation of the same city locked in time.

Industry observers note that the premise of GTA VI is simple on the surface. The game follows Lucía Caminos and Jason Duval in the criminal underworld of Leonida, a fictionalized state based on South Florida: Miami becomes Vice City, the Everglades are the Grassrivers. But its portrayal of real-life hardships, socioeconomic inequality, and even Lucía and Jason’s love story, among other elements, has elicited deeper reflections and responses across our increasingly blurred online and physical worlds.

According to recent reports, to help make sense of these tensions, I got on a phone call with soto and Leo Castañeda, two Miami-based artists whose work I admire. Castañeda is an artist and video game designer exploring Latin American Surrealism in the digital age, and soto co-leads Artists for Artists: Miami, which is leading a boycott of Art Basel next month, and works in the overlapping arenas of labor rights, public infrastructure, and conceptual and social practice.

According to recent reports, our conversation was edited and condensed for clarity. I hope you enjoy it.

It has been revealed that left: Leo Castañeda playing GTA VI, with a mural by Ahol Sniffs Glue included in the game. Right: misael soto's selfie in front of the inside of the clock tower in Assisi (photos courtesy the artists).

Sources indicate that hyperallergic: Before we even get into GTA, I was hoping each of you could tell me a little bit about your relationship to Miami — how long you've been there? How do you feel about living there now?

According to recent reports, leo Castañeda: I moved to Miami first when I was 11. My parents first moved to New York [from Colombia], and then they thought it was too cold, so they moved to Miami. I went to middle school and high school here, then I moved to New York for college, and I moved back in 2015. When I first moved back after college, it was mostly because of the cost of living in New York. And then, within the 10 years that I've been here, it became the same cost of living as New York, except with Florida salaries.

I do feel grateful, though, to be part of the Bakehouse Art Complex, where I have an affordable studio. I live in the North Beach area, and I was able to find a sustainable rent. Miami has a lot of arts nonprofits that help over time. I do feel that, as complicated as the Miami arts ecosystem is, it is pretty supportive — but at the same time, it is tied to all the different layers of money that have come in and dominate the arts, which are very present here.

Industry observers note that misael soto: I moved here right after undergrad. I grew up in South Florida, originally from Puerto Rico, and Miami was always la locura, down south. We would visit my cousins and whatnot from time to time. As I became more and more interested in starting my own practice, I moved down here and have continually been sucked back in. I try to leave, and it pulls me back for whatever reason. Since COVID, everything's changed. Miami became the second most expensive city in the country. The influx was palpable: All of a sudden, there were Texas and California and New York license plates, Teslas zipping around town, and rent just started skyrocketing. There's more flooding. But at the same time, it's gorgeous, and it's special. I live in Mid-Beach. I can go to the water, I can breathe in some sea air, I can hear 10 different languages at once.

It's a really complex relationship with Miami. Especially, I think, both of us make complicated art — we both make art that is unconventional and perhaps even, you could say, difficult to collect. I don't know if you describe yourself that way, Leo, but I definitely do. And making this kind of work in a hyper market-driven neoliberal city like Miami, on the one hand, it gives me a lot of fodder, a lot of material, a lot of things to talk about, as we're doing right now. But at the same time, it can be really frustrating and alienating and lonesome, ultimately.

H: I moved from Argentina to Miami when I was little because my mom got a job there. We lived in the Doral neighborhood, where most people I knew were also from Latin America, until I left for Chicago for college at 18. I've lived in Upcoming York for over a decade now, but I still feel a strong pull to Miami, I feel seen, surrounded by people whose identities are a bit fractured the way I feel mine is.

It has been revealed that and on the note of nostalgia, GTA is a game that was made over the last 13 years, so it chronicles a Miami that’s partly gone. For example, users say Lucía's home is based on a cute salmon-pink, 13-unit condo in Edgewater that was demolished in 2022 to build a 55-story tower, yet it lives on in the game. What does it mean for a video game to preserve a place that no longer exists?

Industry observers note that LC: Well, a few thoughts. During that 13-year development, I would assume the map design was one of the first things they did. But there are also aspects of the chronicling of Miami, or Miami becoming this satire through the game, that have evolved in a shorter time period. For example, this morning I woke up, and there was a Miami Instagram influencer saying that in the fictional version of the Cuban coffee shop Versailles, which is called Antoinette, the bakery has a sign posted outside that says something like, “any politician must pay for all the food when they leave.” That's a reference from a few years ago, when Trump reportedly went to Versailles, ordered food for everyone, and then didn't pay and just walked out.

So it does seem like a video game takes a long time to make, and this one is probably the most ambitious one ever made — 4,500 people working really, really hard, to the point of even having the union situations that they have in the UK branch of the company. But at the same time, I feel like they studied Miami extremely well, and the integration with some local businesses and local artists in particular — I've seen a few street artists like Ahol Sniffs Glue, Soak, Tatiana Suarez, Typoe, as well as musician Nick León. One restaurant is based on Juvia on Lincoln Road, which doesn't exist anymore — they got priced out, and now there's a record of it. The game takes so long to make, but it lives in an ever-present, because it doesn't matter if you made an asset 13 years in the past, like Lucía's apartment, or now; they feel like the present. It's an interesting amalgamation. I would have to spend more time with it to really know: Does this feel like Miami in 2014 or Miami in 2026, or a hybrid?

Sources indicate that H: To get into the politics of the conversation around GTA, I have a lot of icky feelings about one narrative that's taking hold online, which is that the game is “Woke 3.0,” and that the incels and Trump supporters are pissed about it. I only played for a few hours last night, and I went into a gun shop and bought a shotgun. That, to me, panders much more to the NRA hawks and the pro-gun community than to anything that could be considered woke, you know?

It has been revealed that MS: Hmm. I see it the other way around, actually. To me, it's like pretending in order to pacify, in some ways. It's a very complex thing. On the one hand, I remember seeing the woman twerking on the top of a car as the sun came up over the MacArthur. Now that's in the game. And I remember the “face eater” on the MacArthur. I see a man in a thong skateboarding weekly, and now there's a character like that in the game. I teach art history, and I do a whole week on postmodernism and poststructuralism and simulacrum, and the consequences of that, which I think have led us into some really dangerous flattening territory in terms of the role of the artist in the late 20th to early 21st century. I see this game and the way that it's taken over the city in real life and in gameplay, and it makes me think about how much of this is pacifying the role of the artist, or is it pushing through to the other end and becoming a meta-modernist critique that has some gems in there, if you're willing to find them?

It ultimately makes me feel a bit sad in terms of what we deserve. I texted you yesterday, Valentina, when we were talking about having this conversation, and I said, “Well, maybe this is the kind of art the city deserves.” It's not the art that I want for Miami. But in so many ways, Miami is the perfect place. It's been the city for continual use by image makers, from Hollywood to video games.

H: There is some talk about the fact that the game does seem to have an awareness and sensitivity around identity. Cygnus, the curator at the Vice City Museum of Art, is the first non-binary character in Grand Theft Auto history. The actor cast for the role, Jesse James Rose, stated that to prevent anti-trans violence, GTA made it so players would not be able to harm their character. Does this feel like an honest gesture, though?

MS: I was just talking to a friend who's been playing it, and she was like, “Where are all the Haitians?” I remembered there was this huge lawsuit against GTA and Vice City, the one set in the ’80s, from about 20 years ago. Haitian groups sued Rockstar over their portrayal. I did some research, and it seems now the company has shifted. They're saying, “We now punch up as opposed to punching down.” That feels, once again, so uncanny in comparison to the ways in which corporate America has shifted. It makes me think of the phrase, “Black faces in high places won't save us.” I don't want to be lobbing grenades at Rockstar. I think it's fantastic that these changes have been made, especially with such an influential game. But at the same time, it feels like the video game, in its attempt to replicate reality, is lagging in this area.

Industry observers note that H: GTA has a long history of racism. We shouldn't forget that Black characters have been associated with criminality throughout all editions of the game. I haven't played enough to say whether that's the case in the latest version. There is also the question of how the company actually treats its workers, and the labor disputes that are going on behind the scenes. Nestor Uriarte, an animation programmer for Rockstar, wrote an opinion piece for the Guardian where he asked, why is it that with this game that generated billions of dollars, we are still fighting to get union recognition?

Recent findings suggest that MS: I'm curious, Leo, as someone who has been playing games for as long as you have, how you feel about this. I'm a cinephile — I've been one since I was 18, and watched my first Kubrick film the summer before college. And I am dying to see Avengers: Doomsday (2026). I've been following the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) and have been consistently floored by the way they built out this world and the interconnected films. It's history, and it's been making history. But we all know how terrible Disney is. And even with the MCU, they tried to bring in more diversity, and the public didn't respond, so they backtracked on it. I don't know if that analogy holds. But it feels pertinent. It feels similar.

LC: Of course, I have to play more to fully understand it. There's the ads of the game and the game itself. I would say that the Netflix special did feel like it was perpetuating some of the stereotypes of the Haitian community. But at the same time, having played, or seen the range of minority characters so far in the first couple hours, it feels like they have a wide range of personalities, body types, and interests. It's not like they're all criminals. And I also found out that local Haitian muralist Serge Toussaint has his work featured in the game, which I think is an amazing thing. But in terms of artworks in other mediums that really relate to this, this is kind of like, let's say, South Park, or Euphoria — shows that are a mirror to the world that's very explicitly showing you both the best and the worst, and it's making fun of and critiquing everyone. But then how does it flip to show a newly introduced perspective or a solution?

According to recent reports, I've seen a lot of people, especially women game critics and game developers, celebrating the relationship of Jason and Lucía being a central situation in the game, as opposed to a cast of different men from different backgrounds, or, in GTA IV, the Eastern European guy in the seedy underground. Having the relationship and the cultivating of the relationship be a core mechanic, almost in a Sims-like way — and even the learning of emotional labor, or doing kind things around the house, or the game having a really interesting reward mechanic for the nonviolent interactions ... At least in my experience so far, three hours in, I haven't shot a single shot.

H: Wait, how did you save Donnie in the first mission without shooting people?

Industry observers note that LC: Oh, by hiding. It was saying, “Crouch around to make sure no one sees you.”.

Industry observers note that H: I think it's fascinating how different players can make these different decisions. I'm not very good at gaming, so I gave my husband the controller. I was like, “Get us out of here as quickly as possible. I want to get to Vice City!”.

Industry observers note that LC: Yeah, and usually my criticism of Rockstar Games and also Naughty Dog, two significant companies that have these cinematic, movie-like games, is that the story missions often have a path where you fail if you don't take a violent action. The emergent gameplay — which happens just by walking around, the dynamic gameplay that's not in a story mission — is usually extremely layered and nuanced and can go in any direction, violent or not. Again, I'm only three hours in with GTA VI, but so far I appreciate that it is giving the choice of not using violence, and kind of rewarding it. There's something interesting about that. Because usually in those Rockstar games, I'm like, okay, there's this emotional tale, and now there's a mission, and I have to kill 20 minions.

According to recent reports, MS: Leo, I'm thinking about your work and playing your pieces, immersing oneself in these worlds that you create, and there's a kind of mystery in the expansive potential that you create in your installations that at first can be a little overwhelming, but you have to just dive in. And this is the nature of games, or video games. There's a kind of trust fall. And I'm thinking about — let's just go there — the emancipatory potential of that. Because video games, to me, the potential in them as works is the building of awareness, the fostering of empathy, literally embodying someone who has a different way of life or a different body, a different perspective. Especially in our era of political correctness, and a lot of it is warranted, we're asked to speak from our own perspective and not assume things of others. And so this allowance — I wonder how you see the potential in that, especially in something like this game that is so immersive.

LC: I think games as artworks are, to a certain extent, some of the most affordably accessible. Yes, you need to have a PC or PlayStation or Switch or something, but they could be pieces of art that are globally accessible in an immediate way, and they really can affect culture. In terms of empathy, you're controlling a being that you identify as “I”: “I” drove the boat today, or in my game, “I” was camouflaging with the environment to gain energy. There's something there about the mutability of the body, or how one could shift one's self-identity into multiple beings, that is interesting in games, and also interaction and choice as a place that could be art, in a way that performance art also does, and maybe theater. And visual arts in general, maybe in a less touch-based way. But in terms of the empathy, I've been seeing a lot of reviews of GTA VI saying it's actually leading people towards that. Perhaps it is through the romantic relationship [between Jason and Lucía], or maybe by having so much freedom to do whatever you want and kill whoever you want, but then developing these characters and NPCs to a level where they feel like real people.

Recent findings suggest that H: There is one moment in the game that was very emotive in a way that might provoke empathy, and it certainly did for me. At the very beginning — so this is not really a spoiler — we're shown the backstory of how Lucía gets arrested. She's been sitting at a cafe, a little Cuban cafecito, and she's just ordering ice water. The server keeps coming up to her and asking if she wants something else, and she's like, “No, no, just ice water for me.” It's clear that she just can't afford anything else. So in an act of true desperation, and from a place of deep poverty, she decides to rob a payday loan store nearby, and she gets caught. At one point, you can hear the cops saying, “She's saying she left something at the cafe.” And then we see the owners of the coffee shop taking care of her baby, who is then taken by social services.

Industry observers note that we're not shown Tomás, her little baby, at the beginning. It's something that the game surprises us with. To me, it was such a thoughtfully articulated moment.

LC: The beginning is so strong. And then having the tutorial on how to walk and use the camera be her nine months later in prison. Out of overcapacity, the prison is letting some people who have lower sentences perhaps have probation, so she's gonna be let go, but the woman who works there says she doesn't know if or when Lucía will see her baby again. That works as a narrative tool, a teleology, giving purpose to the game beyond, “Oh, she's just a digital girlfriend.” Now there's this question of what the rewards of behavior are that the game's gonna have when one is part of the criminal underworld, but there is a child in foster care that could be taken back or not. That's gonna be so interesting if that ends up being a fork in the road within the narrative, because many of these games have multiple endings.

It has been revealed that MS: This is so fascinating to me in regards to something we were talking about earlier — whether reality is informing the simulacrum and vice versa. It makes me think of how, living in Miami, it continuously feels like maybe the most neoliberal city I've ever lived in. But in so many ways, it oftentimes feels like when you're on the road or when you're at a cafe, you're alone. You really have to fend for yourself in this city. Of course, there are these moments where you break through, or if you're a regular at Enriqueta's, you know who to talk to, this and that. It makes me wonder how the game might change the way that we see ourselves. And, following that thread, how might it actually make us more united?

I don't know if that's a bit of a stretch, but there are just so many people playing this game. And I think over time it's really going to show, as visitors come and reflect their years of gameplay back to the city. In the same way that folks experience Paris syndrome, what will the GTA Miami syndrome be? How might that change us? I was thinking about it for the worse, but how might it change us for the better? Because I don't know a Miami where that childcare situation in the GTA story would happen. Of course, I'm not a caregiver. I'm not a parent. But I don't know that Miami — and I've been here long enough and I have a lot of family here, chosen family. So that makes me, in a weird way, hopeful.

LC: I think it's interesting, let's say with Pop art and conceptual art — if you use a urinal or a fluorescent light, you think of urinal, Duchamp; fluorescent light, Dan Flavin, etc. These artists are claiming this thing from the world. And it's interesting to have this very fluid cycle of, let's say, the Only in Dade Instagram account becoming almost a live feed of GTA, or us within Miami filtering our experience — when there's a very special or odd moment, it being a rehearsal for the game, or the game getting reflected back in the world.

It has been revealed that if the game is marketing itself as this debauched, wild place, and that lures millions and millions of people in, but then it ends up being this profound story that actually highlights how South Florida has complications of income inequality and climate change ... There's a hurricane system in the game, so there's a very strong chance that there will be flooding. Will that situation, where violence and comedy, or things that are not explicitly telling people what the values should be, actually make them more subtle and implicit? Does that create change or not?

H: We've been speaking over an hour, we could probably talk for two more hours. This feels like a beautiful note to end on. But I want to ask if there are any burning observations you want to share.

MS: I feel like we should speak about the takeover of Miami in the real world, physically. Anybody trying to do anything — F1, Art Basel, all these people who come in and take over the city, as they've done for decades — if they want to gain favor with locals, just look at what they did with GTA. Because the amount of free advertising — I mean, I went to this GTA VI-themed drag night, and it was not sponsored by them. It was at Las Rosas. They had a pool table and some neons, and they had the beer from the game available for purchase, but the event itself was fully done just to hop on the bandwagon, and everybody was lapping it up. But at the same time, I'm just very, very impressed, and scared, by the power of putting it everywhere to the point where it was inescapable. It's been inescapable for the last week. It's very impressive.

Industry observers note that LC: Yeah. I've met at least two or three people who have been working on some of the release parties. So they're employing local artists and local musicians and local businesses, as opposed to, as misael was saying, these people arriving out of nowhere, renting a place for really exaggerated prices, and not giving back to the local community. At least through employment. We'll see over time if and how it leads to other forms of sustainability locally. I have a photographer friend who, similarly to that drag show, started doing GTA-style photos in front of one of the latest signs and probably made some money through that, unofficially. So that's interesting.

Industry observers note that MS: I think there's many ways to be a capitalist, or to do this kind of thing and take over the city in this way. And I've never seen something so thoughtful. It honestly reminds me to some degree of the first couple years of Art Basel, when they would do a lot of public programming and free concerts and they really seduced us ... But that's another conversation. I'll stop there.

Tech Report: Meet Harry Nuriev, Bjarke Ingels' pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1577 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Jenia Filatova unless stated.
  • MAJOR founder Bjarke Ingels has selected Harry Nuriev for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler.
  • Nuriev established his studio, Crosby Studios, 12 years ago with the aim of shaking up the world of interior design.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Jenia Filatova unless stated.

MAJOR founder Bjarke Ingels has selected Harry Nuriev for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, the New York and Paris-based designer explains how he constantly aims to reinvent himself and his work.

Nuriev established his studio, Crosby Studios, 12 years ago with the aim of shaking up the world of interior design.

“First, it came from this game of rejection,” he told Dezeen from his house in Tuscany.

According to recent reports, “Let’s say everyone likes to use wood – I won’t have any wood. If everyone likes beige or brown – I won’t have beige or brown. People are confused with a material, so that’s exactly the material I’m going to use.”.

Sources indicate that “I’ll bring exterior to interior, interior to exterior,” he continued. “I’ll mess everything. My colours will be inspired by fashion, my texture will be inspired by architecture.”.

Sources indicate that “You can’t be safe. You always have to risk.”.

Over a decade later, the strategy appears to have worked. Nuriev was recently named Designer of the Year at French design show Maison&Objet and has a client list that many designers would envy. Among his recent works are a sofa for Balenciaga, a pop-up store for Skims, a reflecting pool for Gucci and a puffer-jacket-filled virtual sofa for Nike.

Now Ingels, arguably the world’s best known architect, has selected him as the designer that he believes will have the biggest impact over the next 20 years, as part of our fresh series marking 20 years of Dezeen.

Nuriev established his own studio after freelancing and working on other people’s projects for many years, with the aim of being able to pursue his own creative interests.

Recent findings suggest that “When you work freelance just to pay bills, you don’t really have particular voice,” he remarked. “You have nothing really too specific to express.”.

“I was like, hold on, I actually need to pull all the things together to express myself, whether it’s comfortable for everyone or not.”.

At the time he established his studio, Nuriev recalls the interior design landscape being constrained and dominated by a couple of key, predominant styles that he was determined to break out of.

According to recent reports, “Twelve years ago interior design was just minimalistic Japanese style or classic,” he stated. “Maybe there were some alternative, very vague and obscure styles, but there was literally just two, maybe two and a half camps.”.

“I remember that in interior design, and in particular the industrial area, there was no room to express yourself in a fashion or an art way,” he continued.

“[I realised] there is no way that everyone needs to live the same way, have the same living room and sit in the same sofa. I thought that I will create something different.”.

It was really a big experiment. In retrospect, looking back now, I really think I was lucky.

Rather than identify a target market or clients that wanted a particular style, Nuriev simply set out to create his own individually styled interior spaces and objects.

“It was really a major experiment,” he noted. “In retrospect, looking back now, I really think I was lucky.”.

“By then I had learned classic and traditional way of doing it, so I knew the marble game and wood game and all of the, let’s say, Architectural Digest alphabet. But my idea was that my personal voice, my internal conversation, was very different, I didn’t know if people would like it or not,” he continued.

“Then, to my surprise, some people liked it.”.

Much of Crosby Studio’s work utilises stainless steel, and has an appearance that is cold and almost uncomfortable. However, although this aesthetic is now associated with the studio, Nuriev is keen to ensure that his work continues to evolve.

“I understand we’re responsible for this whole stainless steel, futuristic, uncomfortable, Instagramable aesthetic,” he remarked.

“In a certain way we keep in our DNA our signature things that people already liked, even though they’re kind of retired for me and maybe I want something different,” he continued.

But we always experiment because that’s the part of the formula, part of the recipe, to always have this little spice in every project.

“But we always experiment because that’s the part of the formula, part of the recipe, to always have this little spice in every project.”.

His metallic, almost cold aesthetic is partly born of the idea that you can create spaces that people can be enjoy without necessarily being comfortable.

In a recent development, “It’s bullshit because there’s no such a thing [as comfort],” he said. “I remember after a nightclub at 2am, sitting on a sidewalk, eating some hot dog and being extremely happy, but also I remember being in the most refined, beautiful restaurant, sitting in the most comfortable chair with soft cushioning and feel miserable.”.

Industry observers note that “I developed this mentality that comfort is actually not really healthy,” he continued. “Sitting comfortably in a sort of like sleeping environment, where you can relax all the way, can pull the strength out of you.”.

The competition to create something new and attention-grabbing has intensified in the past 10 years, but Nuriev believes that it is still possible to find new ways of reinventing materials and forms through a process of experimentation and reinvention that he calls “transformism”.

Sources indicate that “[I tell myself] ‘don’t fool yourself, you can’t create anything new, Harry,'” he mentioned. “What you can do, you can find an existing thing and you can reinvent it. You can find a new life.”.

“I’m trying to find new materials, and it’s becoming harder and harder because we explore quite a lot of different things, but surprisingly, there is always something,” he continued.

“It’s like music – every year there is new songs, there is new combinations of the same notes that we have known since Mozart, Bach and Chopin, but it’s still different.”.

After more than a decade, Nuriev has a clear idea of his and Crosby Studio’s strengths, as well as the limitations of his creations.

“They are dessert-ish in their nutrition level, kind of like the entertaining side,” he said. “You don’t expect a full meal from Crosby.”.

According to recent reports, “You come to experience emotion,” he continued. “You want to have this sweet or salty or spicy something, and then you get it and you go. It’s not a daily situation.”.

He believes that his work translates best at the medium scale – an installation, store, room or hotel lobby.

My nightmare is to become a replica of my own self and just retire, becoming an established artist who just found his own voice and just puts his signature everywhere.

Sources indicate that “I think I have found my scale,” he said. “We work in major development projects, which is fine. We can deliver it easily, but there are so many great people who can do it better than us.”.

“Rather than we just distribute all our juice everywhere, and then maybe it will have less energy, [for example in] a huge building, let’s just do this lobby so crazy that people will feel the emotion.”.

As Crosby Studios has established its reputation, the profile of its clients has risen considerably to include some extremely well known and demanding brands, though Nuriev indicates these projects can be the most creative.

Sources indicate that “The calibre of clients is changing dramatically,” he said. “And you know it’s just like in a computer game, you feel like you’re on a different level, they speak in different vocabulary, it’s just complete different game.”.

“Now I’m working with big sharks, and obviously their expectation is different. They’ve been working before me with bigger artists, so it’s also challenging. But this is the challenge of growing.”.

Nuriev believes his most crucial role at Crosby Studios now is to maintain the “rebellious spirit” that it was debuted with – something that inevitably becomes harder as a studio grows and the clients change.

“I think the game now is to constantly remind myself that we’re not an Armani Casa with steel, no matter how old we are, and to keep this spirit,” he stated.

“I think that’s my job as the founder to remind my team, yes, we have gained professional skills, we know how to talk to people, we know how to draft a contract, we know how to deliver on time, but nevertheless, we still want to keep our rebellious spirit.”.

His biggest fear? Becoming a pastiche of himself and rolling out designs in an unchanging signature style.

“My nightmare is to become a replica of my own self and just retire, becoming an established artist who just found his own voice and just puts his signature everywhere. This is not what I want.”.

Industry observers note that “As Coco Chanel stated, once you feel comfortable, it’s the time to change completely. So to reinvent yourself is an exercise, and it’s pretty much my daily life.”.

Today is Dezeen’s 20th birthday, and to celebrate we launch our 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler.

For the series we’ve asked 20 architects and designers who have had a major impact over the past 20 years to each select an architect or designer that they believe will have the biggest impact over the next 20 years.

Called 20×20, the project aims to celebrate the past 20 years of Dezeen while looking forward to the names and faces we’ll be seeing much more of in the next 20 years.

We’ll be revealing the selected architects and designers on Dezeen over the next four weeks, getting to know them and their work in a series of interviews.

The series launches today with a profile of Russian-born, Paris-based designer Harry Nuriev, who was selected by Danish architect Bjarke Ingels.

He will be followed by the selections of Es Devlin, Faye Toogood, Francine Houbine, Frida Escobedo, Huberto Campana, Iris van herpen, Jeanne Gang, Kelly Wearstler, Lesley Lokko, Ma Yansong, Marc Newson, Mariam Kamara, Marina Tabassum, Nendo, Neri&Hu, Patricia Urquiola, Sabine Marcelis, Sou Fujimoto and Yasmeen Lari.

All of the interviews will be listed below as they are published:.

SOM completes first phase of Philadelphia train station restoration

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (384 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architecture studio SOM has completed the first phase of the renovation of the William H Gray III 30th Street Station in Philadelphia, USA, “breathing new life” into the 1930s beaux arts main train hall.
  • Sources indicate that the project saw the renovation of the main train hall, a beaux arts Graham, Anderson, Probst & White building completed in 1931 with a grand limestone facade and Corinthian columns.
  • The hall is on the National Register of Historic Places, greatly restricting the changes that can be made to the structure and its interiors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Lucas Blair Simpson.

Architecture studio SOM has completed the first phase of the renovation of the William H Gray III 30th Street Station in Philadelphia, USA, “breathing new life” into the 1930s beaux arts main train hall.

Sources indicate that the project saw the renovation of the main train hall, a beaux arts Graham, Anderson, Probst & White building completed in 1931 with a grand limestone facade and Corinthian columns. It serves as a major transit hub for the Northeastern United States.

The hall is on the National Register of Historic Places, greatly restricting the changes that can be made to the structure and its interiors.

Keeping to the historic details, including the art deco chandeliers that hang from the tall ceilings, SOM restored the space with builder Gilbane through renovation and a series of specific interventions.

Chief among these was the moving of ticketing, bag drop-off, and other facilities that had been placed in the main train hall into a little-used northern wing of the building.

“Our restoration and repositioning presents an extraordinary opportunity to leverage the station’s strengths, while breathing new life into this beloved building,” said SOM Partner Colin Koop.

This move freed up more room for seating and through traffic in the main hall.

Working with retail partner Nelson Worldwide, SOM also revamped the concessions in the south concourse.

SOM worked closely with US rail system operator Amtrak on the project, which includes offices for Amtrak in the upper levels of the building.

It is part of a wider renovation SOM declared for the station and surrounding areas in Philadelphia in 2016, which included a number of tall buildings. The status of these upcoming structures is unclear.

SOM noted the efforts in preserving the character of the structure.

“We are preserving its historic character while positioning the station for the next generation of travelers to come,” noted SOM Principal Phil Wessell.

“As part of our broader work along Amtrak’s Northeast Corridor, this revitalization reinforces the station’s role as both a vital transportation hub and a defining civic space for Philadelphia.”.

SOM also led the renovation of Daniel Patrick Moynihan Train Hall in New York in 2021, with plans for a Penn Station renovation released earlier this year by PAU.

Russian strikes damage historic buildings in Kyiv and Odesa, including World Heritage sites

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Multiple heritage sites in Ukraine were damaged by Russian strikes on 19 and 20 November, including the Unesco-listed St Michael’s Golden-Domed Cathedral and Monastery complex and St Volodymyr’s Cathedral in Kyiv, known for its frescoes, as well as 12 cultural heritage sites in Odesa, the strategic port city on the Black Sea, which was hit a day earlier.
  • At least nine people were killed in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine during the hours-long attack on 20 November.
  • “Today, Russian drones damaged one of the most famous monuments of our country, the Volodymyr Cathedral,” Tetyana Berezhna, Ukraine’s deputy prime minister for humanitarian policy and minister of culture, wrote in a Facebook post on 19 November after the cathedral in Kyiv was hit, breaking windows and frames and causing “some damage to the paintings and structural elements”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Multiple heritage sites in Ukraine were damaged by Russian strikes on 19 and 20 November, including the Unesco-listed St Michael’s Golden-Domed Cathedral and Monastery complex and St Volodymyr’s Cathedral in Kyiv, known for its frescoes, as well as 12 cultural heritage sites in Odesa, the strategic port city on the Black Sea, which was hit a day earlier. The entire historic centre of Odesa was added to Unesco’s list of endangered World Heritage sites in 2023.

At least nine people were killed in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine during the hours-long attack on 20 November.

“Today, Russian drones damaged one of the most famous monuments of our country, the Volodymyr Cathedral,” Tetyana Berezhna, Ukraine’s deputy prime minister for humanitarian policy and minister of culture, wrote in a Facebook post on 19 November after the cathedral in Kyiv was hit, breaking windows and frames and causing “some damage to the paintings and structural elements”.

According to recent reports, the neo-Byzantine St Volodymyr Cathedral, built in the 19th century, is under the jurisdiction of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU), which broke with the Moscow Patriarchate and was granted autocephaly by Constantinople in 2018. Three of Russia’s most famous artists of the 19th century and early 20th century—Viktor Vasnetsov, Mikhail Vrubel and Mikhail Nesterov—created religious art for St Volodymyr’s, as did the Ukrainian artist Mykola Pymomenko, a teacher of Kazimir Malevich.

The Austrian embassy, located next-door to St Volodymyr's Cathedral, was also damaged. Kyiv's municipal cultural heritage department published an inventory of damage from the attack, which also includes the embassy of the Netherlands.

A Russian drone was shot down over St Michael’s, which is the headquarters of the OCU, on 19 November.

Berezhna’s post cites the cumulative damage from Russia’s accelerating attacks: “Since the beginning of this year, the number of monuments damaged by Russia has increased by more than a third, and by the end of October it was almost 2,200. Almost 2,700 cultural institutions were also affected.”.

The minister was in Lutsk, a historic city in northwestern Ukraine, this week to plan for a conference marking the 600th anniversary in 2029 of the Congress of Lutsk, which brought together the regional monarchies of the time. A Russian strike on Lutsk in October damaged Ukraine’s largest painting, Cosmogony, a 2,000 sq. m work by the contemporary artist Petro Antyp.

Unesco has condemned the latest attacks, especially on Odesa, “which hit the centre of the city, within the boundaries of the World Heritage property ‘The Historic Centre of Odesa’” and “reportedly caused damage to several heritage buildings, including the Kalio Palace, a monument of national importance,” according to a statement released by the organisation. The Kalio Palace, built in 1834, is attributed to the Swiss Italian architect Giorgio Torricelli.

It has been revealed that the strikes came amid escalating tensions and a diplomatic chasm that appears to be widening. The Russian President Vladimir Putin remarked this week that the Kremlin would not negotiate any partial ceasefire or deal with Ukraine after it struck and incapacitated the Kerch Bridge linking mainland Russia to Crimea, a symbol of Russia’s annexation of the Black Sea peninsula in 2014, on 16 and 17 November. At the same time, US President Donald Trump claimed that peace, largely on Russia’s terms, is within reach and reportedly urged European leaders to stop funding weapons for Ukraine. Trump, Putin and the Chinese President Xi Jinping signed a “peace declaration” on 20 November at a trilateral summit hosted by Xi in Shenzhen, China.

In a recent development, A petition to “safeguard Ukraine’s cultural heritage and artistic integrity” was launched last month by the curator Konstantin Akinsha and Bjorn Geldof, the artistic director at Kyiv’s PinchukArtCentre. It calls “for immediate sanctions and the suspension of Russian state participation in international cultural events”. Rapporteur, a Brussels-based policy publication, reported this week that ten European countries are seeking to keep Russia out of the 2027 Architecture Biennale. Russia’s participation in the 2026 Venice Biennale set off a series of protests.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The sun sign is the *it girlie* of the “big three” elements in astrology.

But do you know about your moon sign and rising sign?

We chatted with an astrologer to understand what they are and how to calculate them.

According to Olga Verkhotina — astrologer and personal coach — the substantial three in astrology are your three most significant chart elements:.

“While a natal chart contains so many more intricate details beyond just three elements, the significant three is a way to determine the main highlights that make up your personality and overall temperament,” Verkhotina indicates.

Verkhotina explains that a rising sign is the zodiac sign that falls at the beginning of your First House — basically, the beginning of your natal chart.

“The First House in astrology is associated with a person’s identity, individual activity, even their appearance, and the sign that houses that theme gives its characteristics,” she says.

“Knowing your rising sign describes the way others may perceive you, the way your behavior comes across, as well as how you approach fresh situations in life.”.

You’ll need: date, time and place of birth.

“Knowing the accurate time is crucial here because even 10 minutes can make a difference in the sign,” Verkhotina explains.

“Once you have the data, you can trust astrology software to calculate it for you. There are a lot of natal chart calculators online, so you can just search ‘rising sign calculator,'” Verkhotina says.

Pro tip: Verkhotina suggests reading horoscopes from your rising sign instead of your sun sign, saying it will likely give more personalized insights on which areas of your life might be impacted by current cosmic events.

“A moon sign describes the position of the moon on the zodiac wheel at the moment of your birth,” Verkhotina says.

She explains that the moon in astrology symbolizes:.

“The moon sign helps you better understand how these themes demonstrate themselves in your life,” Verkhotina states.

Unlike the rising sign, you don’t have to have the precise time of birth to know your moon sign, although Verkhotina says it’s still recommended.

You can also use an online calculator to find your moon sign or refer to the ephemeris — a table showing the daily positions of planets.

Verkhotina describes the sun sign as the most crucial planet in your chart.

“It’s the center of your vitality, your ego, consciousness, and individuality at its core. That’s why it’s the most commonly known element in astrology,” she says.

It represents the zodiac sign the sun was in at the time of your birth, which Verkhotina says gives your individuality certain qualities associated with its specific sign.

“It’s important to understand that although the sun is a huge element in astrology, it doesn’t cover the nuances of one’s character,” Verkhotina explains.

Instead, she claims it just represents overall traits.

According to recent reports, verkhotina adds that the specifics of your character are covered in the rest of your astrological chart. “This is why sometimes no two leos are the same,” she indicates.

This one is easy peasy — you don’t have to have your time or place of birth.

“The sun cycle is very similar every year, so you can look it up by the date, month and year of your birth. Each sign corresponds to a calendar date that year,” Verkhotina says.

Here’s each astro sign, in a nutshell, according to Verkhotina.

Your sun sign is important, but your moon and rising signs add extra details.

Your rising sign reflects your identity and how others see you, while your moon sign reveals your emotions and behavior.

To find these signs, you can use online birth chart calculators. Just make sure you have your birth date and time handy for accurate results.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Perron overhauled the kitchen for a longstanding client, with whom the studio has worked on several professional and personal projects over the years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Paul Dussault.

A dedicated space for preparing tea has been placed at the heart of this Canadian house’s renovated kitchen, designed by local studio Perron.

Perron overhauled the kitchen for a longstanding client, with whom the studio has worked on several professional and personal projects over the years.

Her residence sits along the south shore of the St Lawrence River, overlooking Quebec City on the opposite bank.

The view across the water, and the client’s love of tea, were the primary guiding elements for the renovation project.

“For this house, we were not simply working from a checklist of requirements,” noted Perron founder Nathalie Perron.

“We already knew about our client’s lifestyle, energy and the things that are most key to her.”.

The kitchen space was divided into three zones: a space for tea, a central cooking area and a counter overlooking the river.

At the entrance, a small counter wrapped in glossy oxblood red tiles and a partition of burgundy steel bars form a niche that the client has nicknamed her “teahouse”.

Custom lacquered MDF wall shelves store and display cups, saucers, mugs and teapots that she has collected during her travels over the years.

“Each one evokes a specific memory and now has a place in her daily life,” mentioned Perron.

An on-demand hot water tap is also installed within this niche, creating a dedicated space for the tea-making ritual.

The main kitchen area revolves around an angular island, which has space for a bar stool and incorporates a built-in electric stove.

Above, a cylindrical burgundy-hued range hood is framed within more steel bars, suspended from the ceiling to support shelves.

Rows of glass blocks are stacked between the upper and lower cabinets, which are both faced in stained white oak.

Ultra-thin steel shelves hang from the upper millwork, adding extra storage without blocking the light through the translucent bricks.

Opposite, a long counter faces the river through a large window, allowing the homeowner to witness passing ships and changing light conditions as she stands working or washing dishes.

Cristallo quartzite from Brazil forms the countertop and a backsplash.

Long, narrow Cotto Manetti terracotta tiles cover the floor, echoing the shapes of the matte and gloss pink Farblok ceramic tiles by Quintessenza that run up the wall in stripes.

A Mousse wall fixture by Quebec lighting brand JETA adds another feminine touch to the kitchen.

“It is a house that reflects a woman who enjoys going on adventures, but who has created a home that she loves returning to,” noted the studio.

Perron has offices in Montreal and Quebec, the latter in an early 20th-century building renovated to house a studio, showroom and Nathalie Perron’s home.

See more innovative kitchens in our Dezeen Lookbooks series, including examples with striking islands, open storage, natural wood finishes and no wall cabinets.

#34120. Industry News: “We're not saying they're perfect” states architect fighting to save Melbourne's public housing blocks

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1523 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dezeen ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: “We're not saying they're perfect” states architect fighting to save Melbourne's public housing blocks

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its plan to demolish all of Melbourne’s public housing towers.
  • Declared by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne’s public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with new housing by 2051.
  • Sources indicate that officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Ben Hosking, Michael Pham.

Architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its plan to demolish all of Melbourne’s public housing towers. In this interview, he sets out why he believes retrofit is the smarter approach.

Declared by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne’s public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with new housing by 2051.

Sources indicate that officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives. They claim the towers do not meet modern standards and cost too much to maintain, and that the redevelopment programme will triple housing capacity and improve the quality of homes.

But the policy has proved highly controversial, with critics particularly angry about a lack of transparency or consultation with residents, who are being relocated.

It is now subject to an ongoing legal dispute, has prompted concern from the UN’s special rapporteur on housing, and become a political issue in the build-up to the Victorian state election later this month.

Among the voices leading calls for a change of course is Melbourne not-for-profit research and design practice Office.

Office has worked pro bono to make the case for refurbishing the towers, after learning from residents that the government has not published feasibility studies for keeping any of the condemned estates.

“We thought that was pretty odd that you wouldn’t do a refurbishment study on these estates,” Office director Simon Robinson told Dezeen.

“So we took it upon ourselves to start to do these feasibility studies, along with public housing residents.”.

According to recent reports, “We’re not saying that they’re in perfect condition,” he added. “We’re also not saying that all of them should be refurbished – perhaps some are beyond repair. All we are saying is that these refurbishment studies need to occur.”.

In fact, feasibility studies have been conducted by the government but not been made public, despite requests by the Victorian Legislative Council.

By avoiding the relocation of residents, Office estimates that a retrofit and infill approach would cost around $300 million less than demolition and rebuild.

“As all the estates are occupied, the cost of relocating and housing the residents during construction work needs to be included in the project cost; this is consistently excluded and never disclosed,” said Robinson.

“We have estimated that these costs are very significant, with reports indicating that the government is spot purchasing or head-leasing properties from the private market.”.

The practice has put together a counter-proposal based on a strategy that it calls Retain Repair Reinvest (RRR).

RRR focuses on retaining buildings without displacing residents, carrying out renovation work to improve housing comfort and energy efficiency while reducing construction waste and carbon impact.

In a recent development, robinson agrees that most of Victoria’s existing public housing buildings are currently not fit for purpose – buildings are rundown, cold in winter, and sweltering in summer. But he believes comfortable living standards can be achieved through renovations.

Office has applied its RRR strategy to three Melbourne estates in hypothetical case studies – Ascot Vale Estate, Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.

Formerly home to approximately 1,500 people, Flemington Estate’s four towers make up about 10 per cent of Victoria’s high-rise public housing stock.

Only about 32 households remain, though an injunction prevents Homes Victoria from serving further eviction notices while legal challenges are pending.

Office has proposed retaining the estate’s 720 dwellings and building an additional 577 infill social housing units to increase density.

Newly introduced facades and private balconies would be added, with other upgrades including integrated underground parking, a central communal green space, new heating and cooling systems, improved insulation, new kitchens and bathrooms.

Energy efficiency is another key focus. Double-glazed windows, photovoltaic cells, and water conservation systems would provide a 55 percent reduction of global warming potential compared to the demolition approach, according to Office.

Despite the seemingly obvious benefits, the Victorian government has so far been unmoved by the studies presented by the practice.

Robinson believes the reason lies in the fact that the state government no longer wants to manage public housing.

“When the state government manages public housing, they are responsible for maintaining the buildings and organising upcoming tenants – all the admin that comes with owning a building,” he stated.

As well as the demolitions, also attracting concern is the type of housing proposed for redevelopment under the HRRP.

Rather than like-for-like public housing, the new homes will be “community housing” – developed by private developers, and split between below-market and market-rate rental homes.

Despite still being classed as social housing by the state government, community housing is slightly more expensive, and the tenancy is less secure from eviction.

Robinson believes the term was created to misdirect the public.

“What they’re building is community housing, not public housing, so there’s no longer any public housing being rebuilt in Victoria,” he noted.

“The government is now calling everything social housing, because they don’t want the public to know that it’s no longer public housing,” he continued.

“Victoria has the lowest percentage of public housing stock in Australia, and we’re presently demolishing it all and turning it into private and community housing.”.

In a recent development, the problem is particularly charged in the context of Australia‘s housing-affordability crisis. There are currently over 60,000 people on the waitlist for social housing in Victoria, where social housing accounts for three per cent of all dwellings, below the national average of 4.2 per cent and the OECD average of 7 per cent.

“Public housing serves as foundational social infrastructure that treats shelter as an essential human right,” said Robinson.

“By offering rents permanently capped to income and delivering unmatched security of tenure, it provides an unconditional safety net for society’s most vulnerable households.”.

According to recent reports, office’s work has gained political attention. In November 2023, the Victorian Legislative Council debated the merits of the RRR approach, with the council’s Legal and Social Problems Committee urging the government to reconsider demolition and explore all refurbishment options.

It has been revealed that the team can already claim a small victory. At Ascot Vale Estate, the first RRR case study released by Office, the development was quietly removed from the planned demolitions list on the Homes Victoria website and part of the estate has since been refurbished.

The estate is a collection of 57 three-storey brick housing blocks, built in 1947 and designed by renowned modernist architect and public housing advocate Best Overend during his time with the Housing Commission.

This gave Robinson and his team hope that the government would consider the alternatives if presented with the option.

“We have presented to Homes Victoria, we’ve presented to different ministers as well, and we’ve kind of heard that they are starting to look at retrofit some of their existing building stock,” said Robinson.

“It kind of suggests that perhaps they’re gonna prefer we show all of them. So we released the following studies on Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.”.

However, Barak Beacon Estate has since been demolished, and the construction of the redevelopment is due to complete by the end of the year.

Now the fate of Flemington Tower awaits a ruling from the High Court of Australia following a hearing last month.

A class action filed by Inner Melbourne Community Legal on behalf of public housing residents in North Melbourne and Flemington is on its last appeal, after the Supreme Court of Victoria and Victorian Court of Appeal ruled in favour of demolition.

Meanwhile, the Liberal opposition has pledged to pause the HRRP if it wins office at the upcoming state election.

Robinson hopes he and his team have done enough, and continue to raise awareness about the issue.

“We’ve gotten to a point where we feel we can’t just keep putting out these reports,” he said.

Sources indicate that “The papers we produced are quite dense and not for the general public. So what we’re now doing is translating that work into a series of publications, putting it in bookshops, and making it more accessible for the general public.”.

“We continue interviews with different residents, different advocates, different professionals, speaking with journalists and doing lectures. The idea is to bring awareness to what’s occurring, rather than us doing more reports.”.

He is also calling for a frank discussion in the architecture community about the redevelopment projects, which many of Australia’s prominent studios are working on.

“All the major-name architects are working on these estate renewals, some have even won awards as exemplar projects for these architects to promote their practice in terms of doing public good,” mentioned Robinson.

It has been revealed that “It’s really hard to find anyone who’s willing to talk about why they’re doing it, or is it good, the displacement and environmental complications. We’re alone.”.

Dezeen put Robinson’s claims to the Victorian state government, but was told it could not respond in the lead-up to the election.

Photography by Ben Hosking, Michael Pham.

Sources indicate that part of the beauty of yoga is its accessibility for everyone. Yoga practitioners come in all shapes and sizes and are hella modifiable. If you have overweight, there’s 100% a place for you in the world of downward dogs, crescent lunges, and resting pigeons.

Check out these benefits of yoga for overweight.

Recent findings suggest that for wellness, you’d be hard-pressed to find a more holistic practice than yoga. Your physical and mental health can get a boost from busting out your mat.

The limb-stretching, muscle-engaging, bodyweight-bearing nature of yoga has many physical benefits.

Industry observers note that for starters, yoga may enhance your metabolism. An older study found that people who practiced had greater metabolic efficiency and lower weight than non-yogis.

Industry observers note that it’s clear, too, that yoga’s combo of cardio and strength torches calories. A 160-pound person can burn around 180 calories per hour, popping in and out of poses. A 2021 study revealed that both Hatha and vinyasa yoga led to weight loss, with an average of 3.4 kilograms (7.5 pounds) lost over a 6-month.

Extra strength and flexibility are two other well-known upsides of the practice. Research indicates that even sedentary folks can build these elements of fitness by taking up yoga. One study showed that, after 8 weeks of practicing at least twice a week (180 minutes), people with no prior yoga experience had greater muscle strength, endurance, flexibility, and cardio-respiratory fitness.

According to recent reports, on the surface, yoga might look like mere stretching — but the practice goes far beyond the physical. Yoga engages the mind in all sorts of ways that may have benefits for overweight.

Industry observers note that by training your brain toward calm and focus, yoga sessions encourage mindfulness. A mindful outlook can have far-reaching effects in multiple areas of life, like promoting mindful eating and greater body awareness.

According to recent reports, as a form of self-care, yoga can also promote a healthier body image. In a 2018 study, young adults who made it a habit reported higher satisfaction levels with their bodies. Better self-esteem and motivation have also been linked to the practice.

Then, too, yoga’s stress-relieving effects might follow you off the mat and into the dining room. Some research has found that people who do yoga binge eat less often.

According to recent reports, wanna get started with yoga but aren’t sure how? We got you.

It all starts with setting realistic goals and expectations. If you’ve never practiced before, you won’t be pretzel-ing yourself into challenging poses like scorpion or crow overnight — and that’s OK. Consider setting smaller, step-wise goals, such as attending a 30-minute class twice a week or mastering a few basic poses. Little by little, you’ll work your way up to a more advanced practice.

Industry observers note that it’s also wise to select a class (or video) for beginners. Check your gym or yoga studio’s schedule for introductory sessions, and don’t be afraid to let an instructor know before class that you may need some modifications. Most are happy to provide adaptations to make the class a better experience for beginners.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, if you’re pursuing a yoga practice for weight loss, remember to pair it with other healthy lifestyle practices for best results. Though stretching and holding poses burn calories, yoga might not take you to your weight loss goal alone. A balanced diet, cardio exercise, and sufficient sleep are other keys to achieving a healthy weight.

Industry observers note that yoga stereotypes of scantily clad gym babes in impossible contortions might make you feel somewhat intimidated about in-person classes. If you’re concerned that a gym session will make you self-conscious, start with an at-home practice. (YouTube is a treasure trove of classes and instructors explicitly geared for people with overweight.) All by yourself in your living room, there’s no one to impress.

Recent findings suggest that or, if you’re up for in-person yoga, let your instructor know your needs again. Modifications are always possible.

No matter where you practice, credit yourself for showing up for your health. And, at the beginning of your session, don’t forget to set an intention you find motivating or encouraging, such as “I am caring for my body” or “I am worthy of love and respect.”.

Overweight doesn’t have to be a barrier to taking up yoga. Start small, knowing that you’ll get more comfortable with each session. With all the physical and mental health benefits a yoga practice provides — and all the modifications that make it more accessible — it’s worth a try, regardless of weight.

#34118. Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?
